docs.title: Getting started with Orbitly

docs.text: Getting started with Orbitly Orbitly is a private way for your people (family, friends, a team) to see where everyone is, get arrival and departure alerts, chat, and send an SOS. It runs on a small server that your circle (or the person who looks after your tech) controls, so your locations are not sold or stored by a company. Orbitly was published as OpenFamily before the rename. Apps for Wear OS and Apple Watch are coming. The three roles Who What they do Member Installs the app, joins a circle, shares their location. Circle admin Creates a circle (for example "The Rivera Family"), invites people, sets places and privacy rules for that circle. Server admin Installs and looks after the server. Often the same person as the circle admin. See Running your server. Your first ten minutes 1. Install the app on your phone. On Android your server admin gives you a link; see Installing on Android. 2. Enter the server address your admin gave you (for example https://family.example.com) and tap Connect. 3. Create an account, or sign in. If the server asks for an invite code, use the one you were sent (Invite and join). 4. Create a circle or join one: Create a circle. 5. Allow location "all the time" and notifications, and switch off battery saving for Orbitly: Battery and permissions. 6. Open the map: Locations and the map. Where to go next Setting up the server yourself? Quick start (5 minutes) Normal, Private and server processing in one picture: Concepts Places and arrival alerts Driving reports Chat Privacy modes explained: what the server can and cannot see Safety: SOS and check-ins Removing a person, a lost phone Something wrong? Troubleshooting; FAQ; Glossary All the screenshots in these guides are drawn from the app's own screens with made-up data (the "Rivera Family"). See How screenshots are made.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.summary: What changed in each Orbitly release (published as OpenFamily before the rename), in plain words. The server shows the section for the version it runs on the admin Documents page and on Settings, App…
docs.text: Changelog What changed in each Orbitly release (published as OpenFamily before the rename), in plain words. The server shows the section for the version it runs on the admin Documents page and on Settings, App versions. Older entries are in the git history (git log v0.16.0..); this file starts at v0.17. Each release says which app versions it works with. The server keeps working for the last 5 minor versions of the app (see API compatibility), so you can update the server first and the phones afterwards. Unreleased Fewer surprise sign-outs. One phone has several parts that refresh the sign-in together (the screen, the background location service, a retry). The server treated the third as token theft and signed the person out, which showed up as "Couldn't reach the server". For 10 seconds after a refresh token is used, repeated refreshes now get the same new token. After that, and if the new token was already used, the strict theft rules still apply. v0.25.2 (2026-11-08) Build fixes only: the Android app did not compile in v0.25.0 and v0.25.1 (a key-storage call that does not exist and a deprecated watch listener setting). Same server as v0.25.0. The phone APK, AAB, Wear OS APK and iPhone file are attached to this release. The phone no longer wakes when a watch merely connects while the app is closed; it still wakes for watch commands. v0.25.1 (2026-11-08) Build fixes only: the v0.25.0 Android and Wear OS release files were not produced (code-style checks and a signing-key path in the build scripts). Same app and server as v0.25.0; the files are attached to this release. v0.25.0 (2026-11-08) Works with app versions 0.21 to 0.25. The phone and watch apps are the big change; the server update is safe to apply first. Admin site overhaul. A grouped, collapsible menu with page and settings search, a Settings page with its own section menu and (i) help, new administrator settings (sign-in session lifetime, idle timeout and sessions per person, and the default for members), a Builds page that lists the Android APK and the iPhone IPA (plus the Wear OS watch APK), a System health checklist with a fix hint for every row, a Server processing panel on the Dashboard and Private circles pages, and Fleet health that shows one row per phone with the real app version and 'what to do' hints. Sessions. Signing in again from the same phone replaces its old session instead of adding another, idle sessions expire after 14 days, there is a limit per person, and administrators can sign out sessions in bulk. Phones on low memory. The app picks a profile by the phone's RAM (under 4 GB lite, 4 to under 6 GB standard, 6 GB and up full), trims caches when Android asks for memory, and the release now ships a combined APK plus per-CPU APKs. Faster on mobile data. The server now compresses its answers, the app reuses its connection to the server instead of reconnecting for every request, and unchanged lists come back as a tiny "not modified" answer. Smaller updates. The people list and saved places can be fetched as "only what changed", with a compact view for the map and watch. One start-up request (/app/bootstrap) replaces five. Lighter history. A day's trail can be thinned on the server to as many points as the map can draw; the audit log can be paged. Steadier connection. Reads retry a couple of times with a short random pause when the network blips; writes are never repeated automatically. Optional HTTP QUERY method for multi-window history reads, off by default (QUERYMETHOD=1); the app falls back to POST by itself. Details and the Cloudflare check are in API wire efficiency. Database: places gain an updatedat (migration 000360). Orbitly keeps working when the server is down. The app remembers the last people, positions (with their real age), places, circles, chat and notifications and shows them at once, with a small bar: "Server unreachable. Showing last known. Will sync when it is back." (and Try again). Chat messages, check-ins, Help alerts and SOS written meanwhile are saved on the phone and sent in order, once, when the server is back. An SOS that cannot be delivered says "SOS not sent yet", keeps trying and offers to text your emergency contacts from your own messages app. New movement of other people still needs a server. See "When the server is down". Fixes: a long outage no longer discards the queued location points or queued Private circle messages and check-ins; the app opens within 4 seconds on a dead network and never signs you out because of a network error; Diagnostics counts every waiting update. Server: SOS, Help alerts and check-ins accept an optional clientid so a replay after a lost answer is stored once (database migration 340). Private circles keep sending when the phone is locked. The key that protects your keys on the phone no longer needs the screen to be unlocked (it is still stored in the phone's security chip and can not be copied out). Phones update automatically the first time you open the app after updating. Before this, a phone in a pocket could stop sending to a Private circle. See the threat-model note in End-to-end encryption. Driving tab in Private circles works for members who use the server, and members who keep data on their phone get "Use the server" or "Compute reports on this phone" instead of a dead end. Simpler settings. Settings are grouped (Account, Sharing & privacy, Notifications, Driving & safety, Server & data, Phone health, Appearance, About) with a search box. Each row has one short line; tap the small (i) for the details. Encryption keys, Server processing, Active sessions (This device, Older sessions, Sign out other sessions) and Diagnostics were tidied up. Wording: "circle" instead of "family" where it means friends too. Server: POST /auth/sessions/current tells an app which session is its own. Members are on the server by default; they opt out by hand. On a server set to Home, a member of a circle that has server processing on no longer has to find "Use the server": the next time they open the app, their own phone signs it for them (same signature as a tap, visible in the circle's key log). They see "Your circle uses the server so maps, history and driving reports work. Tap to keep your data on your phone." and one tap on Keep on my phone switches it off and deletes what the server holds of theirs. If they ever chose, nothing is changed again. Not applied automatically: circles that require server processing (they keep their consent card), child accounts, members on an old app (they get it after updating), and servers set to Cloud or not chosen (the app asks instead). Admin: the member default (server or phone, auto-apply on or off; API /api/admin/settings/member-defaults) and a list of members not yet on the server with a message to send (API /api/admin/members-not-on-server). Circle admins see the same list on the circle's processing screen. Joining: the invite preview says "This circle uses the server by default; you can opt out." The server can read the data of everyone on it, as before; this changes who presses the button, not what the server can read. Better Documents page. A topic tree you can collapse, an "On this page" list that follows you as you read, breadcrumbs, previous and next links, search with highlighted matches and recent searches (press /), notes and warnings in colour, code you can copy, pictures you can enlarge, and a layout that works on a phone and prints cleanly. New guides. Quick start (5 minutes), Concepts (Normal, Private and server processing, with a picture), Troubleshooting, FAQ and a Glossary. The privacy and chat pages now say the same thing as the app. Orbitly on Wear OS watches. A watch app for Wear OS 3 and newer (Galaxy Watch 4 and later, Pixel Watch and others) shows your people, sends "I'm OK", SOS (press and hold, 5 second cancel), pause sharing and quick replies, and offers a tile and a watch face complication. The phone stays the only place with your sign-in and Private-circle keys; Settings, Watch shows the connection. Older Tizen Galaxy Watches are not supported. The release gets an extra orbitly-wear-<version>.apk (the phone app keeps its own orbitly-<version>.apk). See Orbitly on your watch. Apple Watch app (watchOS 9 or newer). See your circle on your wrist (name, where, how long ago, battery), a distance and direction arrow, SOS with press-and-hold and a cancellable countdown, I'm OK, pause or resume sharing, quick replies and alerts. Your iPhone keeps your sign-in and keys; the watch only shows what it is sent. New under Settings, Watch. This part is new and was not yet tried on a real watch. v0.24.1 (2026-11-08) Build fix: the v0.24.0 release files were not produced because of a file-name mismatch in the build scripts. Same app and server as v0.24.0, now with the orbitly-<version>.apk, .aab and iPhone files attached. v0.24.0 (2026-11-08) Orbitly. The server does the processing by default. New circles are Normal (the server keeps locations so maps, history and driving reports just work). Private is a clear choice: "only phones can read locations". The server joins by itself. No extra container, no commands, no passwords: the server creates its own key on first start and your phone asks "Your server wants to join - does the code match?". One tap approves it. The setup card is three steps and ends in a green "Server is processing". The old separate container stays available under Details. Use the server (recommended) / Keep on my phone. A one-time question on each member's phone in circles where the admin turned the server on. Nobody is ever switched on for someone else. "Keep on my phone" means locations are shared privately, encrypted from phone to phone, with no reports unless phone reports are turned on. Existing Private circles get a card for the admin: "Let the server do the processing (recommended)". Members on an old app get a "needs update" state and a message to send, and an "Update available" card in Settings. Switch a Private circle back to normal mode in one tap (admin), with a plain explanation of what is deleted and who is told. New Docker volume serverdevice for the server's key (back it up with the database). OPENFAMILYSERVERDEVICE chooses built-in, sidecar or off. Smoother app in Private circles. Decrypting updates no longer blocks the screen, a catch-up draws two map frames instead of hundreds, and each person's last known position is remembered on the phone, so a cold start is never blank. Phone-side driving reports are now an opt-in switch (off by default). Phone health reports arrive. The admin Fleet page shows the real app version, OS, battery and permission state, and treats a Private-circle phone that is sending encrypted updates as alive. OpenFamily is now Orbitly. The app, the admin web, the notifications and the docs use the new name, logo and icon. The project is for any circle of people, family and friends alike. Nothing to migrate: your server, accounts, circles and app installs keep working, and the app updates in place (the Android and iOS package ids and the signing key are unchanged). About screens. Settings, About in the app and in the admin web show the version, the credit "Based on OpenFamily by wheresfrank and contributors (AGPL-3.0)", a link to the source code and the open-source licenses. See Credits and license. Release files are now named orbitly-<version>.apk (and .aab, .spdx.json); older releases keep their openfamily- names and the server downloads either. If you filter releases in Obtainium by name, use orbitly. Some internal names keep "openfamily" on purpose: see Naming. Works with app versions 0.20 to 0.24. v0.23.0 (2026-11-08) "Why can't I see everyone?" In Private circles the app now says why a person has no location (their phone has not sent an update, has not received the key, needs the app updated, or paused sharing) and has a one-tap fix. The phone fetches its circle key on its own, sends a first position as soon as the app opens, and no longer drops queued updates while offline. Add the server in three taps: add, compare the four code groups, OK. The admin picks a home or cloud server profile in Settings; the app uses it to suggest the right default. Encrypted chat in Private circles: messages, edits, deletes and photos go phone to phone and never to the server's processing. Old plaintext history stays readable and an admin can delete it. Documents page in the admin site, with the guides and screenshots that ship with the server, plus an App versions card showing who needs to update. Works with app versions 0.19 to 0.23. Chat encryption needs app 0.23. v0.22.1 (2026-11-07) Maintenance release: removes unused test helper code so the release build passes its checks. No change for families or admins. v0.22.0 (2026-11-07) Per-member privacy ("processing lanes"). In a Private circle every person now chooses for themselves whether their phone also sends data to the server, or keeps it phone-to-phone only. See Privacy modes explained. The circle admin decides whether server help exists for the circle at all; only the person themself can opt in or out of it. Phones compute trips, driving events and the weekly summary on the phone for people who keep their data off the server. The join screen shows how a circle handles privacy before you join. Needs app 0.22 for the new screens. Older apps stay safe: they keep data phone-only and are asked to update. v0.21.1 (2026-11-07) iOS build pipeline fixes (unsigned test builds for sideloading). No change to the server or the Android app. v0.21.0 (2026-11-07) App compatibility window. The server now supports the last 5 minor app versions, shows banners in old apps ("Update required" or "A newer version is available") and lists app versions in use in the admin panel (Settings, App versions). See API compatibility. Family chat improvements. Sends are no longer duplicated when the network is flaky; you can edit and delete your messages; missed messages are fetched after a reconnect. See Chat. Admin setting "Trust this server by default" and matching prompts in the app. v0.20.1 (2026-11-07) Backups to S3 can be set up from the admin panel; saved credentials are tied to their destination and the address checks were tightened (IPv6). A flaky Bubble expiry test was fixed (tests only). v0.20.0 (2026-11-07) Scheduled off-site backups. Optional backup service that writes encrypted copies to S3-compatible storage with retention, and an admin Backups card with a "Back up now" button. See Backup and restore. v0.19.0 (2026-11-06) Home Assistant integration: read-only scoped tokens, signed webhooks, an admin Integrations card and a custom component. See Home Assistant. Reliability tools: phone diagnostics and self-test, "silent phone" and late-arrival alerts, and a fleet health page for admins. Admin web: consistent page layout, better phone layout, new System health page. iOS: Secure Enclave key channel, universal-link route and release workflow. Private circles:

docs.title: Credits and license
docs.summary: Orbitly is a free, open-source fork of OpenFamily, licensed AGPL-3.0; who built it, what it is based on and where to get the source.
docs.text: Credits and license Orbitly is a free, open-source fork of OpenFamily, licensed AGPL-3.0; who built it, what it is based on and where to get the source. Where Orbitly comes from Orbitly is a substantially extended fork of OpenFamily by wheresfrank and contributors. Thank you to the original authors: the first version of the server, the app and the idea of a private, self-hosted way to share locations came from their work. Orbitly was published as "OpenFamily" until the rename to Orbitly; it is the same project and the same code history, nothing was re-started. The name changed because the project is for any circle of people, family and friends alike, and because several unrelated projects are also called OpenFamily. License Orbitly is free software under the GNU Affero General Public License, version 3 (AGPL-3.0). The full text is in LICENSE in the repository. You may use, study, change and share it, and if you share a changed version (or run one for other people as a service) you must offer them its source under the same license. The copyright notices of the original OpenFamily authors are kept; changes and additions belong to their respective contributors. See NOTICE. Source code (AGPL section 13) Everyone who uses an Orbitly server over a network may get the source of the version it runs. The public source is <https://github.com/TheTractorHacker/orbitly> (the address the old TheTractorHacker/openfamily name redirects to). Check out the tag that your server reports under Settings, About. If you run a modified version, you must publish your modified source and point your users to it: change the links in app/lib/brand.dart and web/src/lib/brand.ts before you build. You can find these credits and links inside the products: the app: Settings, About, with the open-source licenses page; the admin web: the footer of every page, the sign-in page, and Settings, About Orbitly. Third-party code backgroundlocator2 (MIT; Copyright 2020 REKAB, Copyright 2022 Yukams): a modified copy is vendored under app/packages/backgroundlocator2 and keeps its own LICENSE. Every Go, npm and Dart dependency and its license is listed in Third-party licenses; the audit is in License compliance. Map data is from OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL). Names that still say "openfamily" Some internal identifiers keep the old spelling on purpose so existing installs keep updating. See Naming.

6. Make it reliable on every phone

docs.text: Quick start (5 minutes) From an empty server to your first shared location: install, sign in, approve the server, create a circle, invite people and install the app. You need a computer that stays on (a small home server, a NAS with Docker, a Raspberry Pi 4 or newer, or a rented server) and a phone. The long version of every step is linked, so you can start here and dig in only where you need to. Tip Pick the name of your circle later. Nothing here is permanent: you can rename a circle, add people and change the privacy mode whenever you like. 1. Install the server (about 3 minutes) On the server, with Docker and Docker Compose v2 installed: git clone https://github.com/TheTractorHacker/orbitly.git cd orbitly ./scripts/setup.sh # asks for your address and admin email, writes .env docker compose up -d --build curl http://localhost:8080/healthz # {"status":"ok"} Answer :80 to the address question for a first test on your own network, or your domain name for the internet. The admin password is shown once: save it in a password manager. More detail: Install the server. For a domain and HTTPS: HTTPS and your own domain. 2. First sign-in Open http://localhost:8080/admin/ (or your domain plus /admin/) and sign in with the admin email and password. Registration is closed, so only people with an invite code can join later. Details: First run. 3. Create an account and a circle in the app 1. Install the app on your phone (Android; on iPhone your admin gives you the install link). 2. Enter your server address, tap Connect, then create an account with the same email as the admin. 3. Choose Create a new family (a circle can be a family, friends, a team) and give it a name. See Create a circle. New circles are Normal: your server keeps locations, so the map, history and driving reports just work. If you want locations readable only by phones, read Concepts first. 4. Approve your server (once) Your server creates its own key the first time it starts. Your phone shows "Your server wants to join" with a short code of four groups. Check that it is the same code as in the admin web under Settings, Server setup, then tap Yes, it matches - approve. The setup card then turns green: Server is processing. Only a server administrator can approve. More: Server setup. Note In a Normal circle the server already processes locations. Approving matters most when you use Private circles and want the server to help for the people who choose Use the server. 5. Invite your people In the app open the circle, tap Invite, then Create invite code, and send the code or link by message. They install the app, enter your server address, choose Join a family and type the code. See Invite and join. 6. Make it reliable on every phone Each person should allow location all the time, allow notifications, and set battery use to unrestricted for Orbitly. Without this, phones go quiet when the screen is off. See Battery and permissions. Check it worked [ ] curl http://localhost:8080/healthz answers ok [ ] You can sign in to the admin web [ ] Your circle shows you on the map [ ] A second phone joined with the invite code and appears [ ] The admin Fleet page shows both phones reporting If something is missing, go to Troubleshooting. Next Set up backups before anything else: Backups and restore Understand the privacy choices: Concepts and Privacy modes explained Words you may meet: Glossary; quick answers: FAQ

docs.title: Concepts: Normal, Private and server processing
docs.summary: The three ways a circle can handle your location, in plain words: who can read it, who does the work, and what that costs.

headings.text: Choice 1: the circle's mode (the circle admin chooses)
Choice 2: who does the work in a Private circle (each person chooses for themselves)

docs.text: Concepts: Normal, Private and server processing The three ways a circle can handle your location, in plain words: who can read it, who does the work, and what that costs. Everything in Orbitly comes down to one question: who can read a person's location, and who does the work of turning it into a map, trips and alerts? There are two choices to make, and they are easy to mix up, so here they are one at a time. Choice 1: the circle's mode (the circle admin chooses) Mode In one sentence Can the server read positions? Normal (the default for new circles) Phones send positions to your server, which does all the work. Yes. Private Phones lock each position with a key the server never has, and only the other phones in the circle unlock it. No. It relays locked data. Normal is the simplest and gives you everything: the live map, history, weekly driving reports, arrival and departure alerts, the admin web's view, and integrations such as Home Assistant. The person who runs the server can in principle read the data, which is why you want to run it yourself or trust whoever does. Whether a server admin may look at members on the admin map is a separate switch, off by default, and every look is written to a log the circle can read. Private is for circles where nobody, not even the person running the server, should be able to read where people are. The price is that the server cannot compute anything from your data, so phones do the work. Choice 2: who does the work in a Private circle (each person chooses for themselves) Inside a Private circle, every member answers one question on their own phone, once: Use the server (recommended): your phone also gives the server a readable copy of your data, so reports, history and the admin web work for you. The rest of the circle still shares locked data with each other. Nobody can choose this for you. Keep on my phone: your data stays locked. Reports are off unless you turn on phone reports, which use more battery. You can change your mind at any time. This is called server processing. It is the default direction of Orbitly (a new circle is Normal and the setup suggests the server), but it is never switched on behind your back. What it costs Normal Private, Use the server Private, Keep on my phone Server can read your position Yes Yes, your copy only No Live map, history Yes Yes Yes (phone to phone) Driving reports and weekly summaries Yes Yes Only with phone reports (more battery) Admin web map If admin access is on If admin access is on No Battery use Lowest Low Higher Offline behaviour Phones keep working without a connection to the server. Position updates wait on the phone and are sent when the connection returns, nothing is dropped, and each person's last known position is remembered on the phone, so a cold start never shows a blank map. Chat drafts stay and are retried without sending twice. The documents you are reading are stored on the server, so they open without internet. Map tiles come from a map provider and need internet unless you host your own (see Self-hosting). Chat Chat in a Private circle is end-to-end encrypted: messages, edits, deletes and photos are locked on the sender's phone and opened on the members' phones. The server only relays them and never reads them, even for people who chose Use the server. Chat in a Normal circle is stored readable on the server, like locations. Old messages from before a circle turned Private stay readable until an admin deletes them. See Family chat. What no choice hides That you use the app and roughly when (the server sees that something was uploaded, its size and time). Anything copied before you changed your mind, and old backups. Other members: anyone in the circle can read what the circle shares. Only add people you trust. Share links work for anyone who has the link until they expire (Sharing links). Where to read more Privacy modes explained: the same ideas with screenshots and "how to choose" Server setup: add your server, approve it once Deployment profile: home or cloud: what to do on a rented server Privacy processing design: the technical decision record

docs.title: Frequently asked questions
docs.summary: Short answers to the questions families and friends ask most, with a link to the page that explains more.
docs.text: Frequently asked questions Short answers to the questions families and friends ask most, with a link to the page that explains more. Basics What is Orbitly? A private, self-hosted way for a circle of people (family, friends, a team) to share locations, get arrival alerts, chat and send an SOS. It runs on a server you control. See Getting started. Is it only for families? No. A circle can be a family, a group of friends, a carpool or a team. Some screens still say "family". Was Orbitly called something else? Yes, OpenFamily. Your server, accounts and circles keep working after the rename. See Credits and license. Does it cost money? The software is free and open source (AGPL-3.0). You pay for whatever runs the server, if anything. Is there an iPhone app? A watch app? Orbitly has Android and iPhone apps. Wear OS and Apple Watch apps are coming; they are not available yet. Privacy Can the person who runs the server see where I am? In a Normal circle the server can read positions. In a Private circle it cannot, unless you choose Use the server for yourself. See Concepts. Can a server admin watch members on the map? Not by default. It is a separate switch (ADMINLOCATIONACCESS), off by default, and every look is logged. See Operator privacy controls. Is chat private? In a Private circle chat is end-to-end encrypted and the server never reads it. In a Normal circle chat is stored readable on the server. See Family chat. Does server processing mean my data is sent to a company? No. "The server" is the one you or your family run, not a service run by Orbitly. Using it Why is nobody on the map? Start with Nobody shows on the map. What happens when the phone has no signal? Updates wait on the phone and are sent when the connection returns. See Concepts. Does it drain the battery? Normal circles use the least; phone-side reports in Private circles use more. See Battery and permissions. Can I pause sharing? Yes, per circle: turn off Share my location. See Create a circle. Does SOS call the emergency services? No. It alerts your circle. See Safety and check-ins. Running the server What do I need? A machine with Docker that stays on, about 1 GB of free RAM and a few GB of disk. See Install the server. Do I need a domain? Not for a test on your own network; phones should use HTTPS on the internet. See HTTPS and your own domain. How do I update? Run the update script on the server; phones can update later because the server supports the last five app versions. See Updating the server. How do I back up? See Backups and restore. Do this before your first update. Something is wrong. See Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.summary: The words Orbitly uses, in alphabetical order, in plain language.
docs.text: Glossary The words Orbitly uses, in alphabetical order, in plain language. Admin web The website that comes with your server, at /admin/. Server admins use it to see circles, phones, backups and these documents. APK The installable file for Android. Orbitly publishes orbitly-<version>.apk with every release. See Android install. Approve the server The one-time tap on your phone that lets your server join your circles as a helper. See Server setup. Audit log A list of who looked at what (for example a server admin viewing a member). Circles can read the log about themselves. Backup A copy of the database saved elsewhere so you can restore after a failure. See Backups. Circle A group of people who share their location with each other: a family, friends, a team. Called "family" in some screens. See Create a circle. Circle admin The person who manages a circle: invites, removes, changes the privacy mode. Not the same as a server admin. Check-in A short message that tells your circle you arrived safely, or that you are fine. See Safety and check-ins. Compose (Docker Compose) The tool that starts the server and its database with one command: docker compose up -d. Fleet The admin web page listing which phones are reporting, with app version, battery and permission state. Geofence / Place A saved spot such as Home or School. Orbitly can tell the circle when someone arrives or leaves. See Places. Invite code A short code or link a circle admin sends so that someone can join. Codes expire. See Invite and join. Keep on my phone Your choice in a Private circle: your data stays locked and only phones process it. See Concepts. Lane The technical word for the choice between "phones only" and "server helps". In the app it appears as Keep on my phone and Use the server. Normal circle A circle where the server can read positions and does the processing: the default for new circles. Private circle A circle where positions are locked on phones with a key the server does not have. See Privacy modes explained. Push notification An alert delivered to your phone even when the app is closed. See Notifications. Release A numbered version of Orbitly (for example 0.24). The server works with the last five minor versions of the app. See App versions. Server admin The person who installs and looks after the server. Often the same person as the circle admin. Server processing The server turns positions into maps, trips, driving reports and alerts. Always on in Normal circles; each person's choice in Private circles. Session A signed-in phone or browser. You can end old sessions under Settings, Security, Active sessions. SOS The button that alerts your circle. It never calls emergency services. See Safety. Two-step sign-in (MFA) A second proof, such as a code from an authenticator app, when you sign in. Recommended for admins.

categories.title: For your circle
categories.description: Using the app day to day, in plain words.

docs.title: Create a circle
docs.summary: A circle is a group of people who share their location with each other: your family, friends, a carpool, the grandparents. You can be in several circles and choose in each one whether you share.
docs.text: Create a circle A circle is a group of people who share their location with each other: your family, friends, a carpool, the grandparents. You can be in several circles and choose in each one whether you share. 1. After signing in choose Create a new family. 2. Give it a name, for example "The Rivera Family". The name is only for your people. 3. Tap Create family. You are the circle admin. 4. Next the app offers to invite your family. See Invite and join. Circle details Open a circle to see its people, who is an admin, your sharing switch and the invite code. Share my location turns your sharing on or off for this circle only. Admins can rename the circle, change roles, remove people and set the circle's privacy mode. Leave removes you from the circle; Delete (admins) removes the circle for everyone. Choosing a privacy mode when you create a circle matters: Normal circles let the server show locations on the admin map and compute driving reports; Private circles keep positions sealed between phones. Read Privacy modes explained before you decide.

docs.title: Invite people and join a circle
docs.summary: How a circle admin invites family or friends with a code or link, and how they join from the app.
docs.text: Invite people and join a circle How a circle admin invites family or friends with a code or link, and how they join from the app. Inviting (circle admins) 1. Open the circle and tap Invite. 2. Tap Create invite code. Share the code or the link by message. Codes expire and can be revoked. A server admin can also see and revoke open invites on the admin web Groups page. Never post an invite code in a public place. Joining 1. Install the app and enter your server address. 2. Choose Join a family and type the code, or just open the invite link on your phone. 3. Before you join the app shows how the circle handles privacy, so you know what you are agreeing to. Read it; see Privacy modes explained. 4. Allow location access (Battery and permissions). If the code is refused: check it was typed exactly, that it has not expired, and that you are on the correct server. Ask the admin for a fresh code.

docs.title: Locations and the map
docs.summary: The map shows each person in your circles with a photo or initial, their battery level, and how fresh the position is.
docs.text: Locations and the map The map shows each person in your circles with a photo or initial, their battery level, and how fresh the position is. Reading the map A bubble is a person. Tap it for their card: address, battery, speed and when the position was last updated. Grey or "last seen" means the phone has not reported for a while. That is usually battery saving, a switched-off phone or no signal, not a problem with you. See Nobody shows on the map. Paused means the person chose to stop sharing for a while. They are not hidden by mistake. See Safety and check-ins. Your circles, people and their addresses also appear as a list: On the web Your server's admin web page has the same map and history for people who prefer a computer. A server admin does not see anyone's position unless the server was set up to allow it; see Privacy modes explained. History Each person's route is stored for a limited time (90 days by default) and each person can choose a shorter time or erase their own history in the app.

docs.title: Places and arrival alerts
docs.summary: A place is a spot you care about, such as Home, school or Grandma's. Add a place and Orbitly tells the circle when someone arrives or leaves.
docs.text: Places and arrival alerts A place is a spot you care about, such as Home, school or Grandma's. Add a place and Orbitly tells the circle when someone arrives or leaves. 1. Open Places and tap Add a place. 2. Search for an address or move the pin, then pick a radius. 3. Choose who is notified and for arriving, leaving or both. Tips: Use a radius of at least 100 m so GPS drift does not cause false alerts. A fix with poor accuracy is ignored for alerts; see Geofence accuracy. A Bubble is a temporary circle around where a person is right now (for example while they walk home); the person is told it exists. See Bubbles. People who have paused sharing do not trigger place alerts.

docs.title: Driving reports
docs.summary: Orbitly can summarise driving each week: number of drives, distance, top speed, and events such as speeding, hard braking, rapid acceleration and (optional, per person) phone use.
docs.text: Driving reports Orbitly can summarise driving each week: number of drives, distance, top speed, and events such as speeding, hard braking, rapid acceleration and (optional, per person) phone use. Reports need driving detection switched on by each driver. Nobody can switch it on for someone else. In a Normal circle the server works the report out from locations. In a Private (phone-to-phone) circle each phone works out its own report and shares only the result, so the numbers can lag and use a little more battery. See Privacy modes explained. Phone use is shown as Off (not zero) for people who have not turned it on. Details and thresholds for administrators: Driving events and Driving sensors.

docs.title: Family chat
docs.summary: Every circle has a chat for its members only, end-to-end encrypted in Private circles.
docs.text: Family chat Every circle has a chat for its members only, end-to-end encrypted in Private circles. Open the Circle tab and tap Family chat. A badge counts unread messages. Type a message and send. If you are offline the draft stays and is retried without sending twice. Long-press your own message to edit or delete it. Circle admins can delete any message. You can send a photo; location data inside it is removed. Notifications say only "New message in <circle>", not the text, unless your server admin enabled verbose notifications. Who can read the chat? In a Private circle chat is end-to-end encrypted: messages, edits, deletes and photos are locked on your phone and opened on the other members' phones, and the server only relays them. In a Normal circle chat is stored readable on the server, like locations. Messages written before a circle turned Private stay readable until a circle admin deletes them. Choosing between modes: Concepts. Technical notes: Chat and Encrypted chat design.

docs.title: Privacy modes explained
docs.summary: Each circle has a privacy mode. This page explains them without jargon: who can see what, and what you give up for more privacy.

headings.text: Server-assisted by default (when your server owner turns it on)
What opting out does not hide

docs.text: Privacy modes explained Each circle has a privacy mode. This page explains them without jargon: who can see what, and what you give up for more privacy. The three modes Mode In one sentence The server can see your position? Normal Your phone sends your position to the server, which shows it to your circle. Yes. Private (phone-to-phone) Your position is locked on your phone and only the other phones in the circle can unlock it. No. It stores locked data only. Server-assisted (a Private circle where you allowed it) Like Private, but your phone also gives the server a readable copy so it can do extra work for you. Yes, for you only. Normal Simple and complete: the server draws the map, works out trips and weekly driving reports, sends arrival alerts, and feeds the admin web and integrations such as Home Assistant. The server's owner can in principle read the data. Whether a server admin may look at members on the admin map is a separate switch that is off by default (ADMINLOCATIONACCESS); every look is written to an audit log the circle can read. Private (phone-to-phone) Positions are encrypted on your phone with a key the server never has. Other members' phones decrypt them. A stolen database or a curious operator sees only unreadable data and metadata (that you uploaded something, and roughly when). What changes: the server cannot compute things from your data, so your phone does it. Trips, driving reports and weekly summaries are calculated on the phone and shared as results. Expect more battery and CPU use and some features arriving later or only after the phone has run them. The admin web can show a Private circle only if the signed-in person is a member and has approved the browser from their phone. In the app's processing screens the phone-to-phone choice is labelled Phone only and the server-assisted choice Processed by server / Let the server process my data. Server-assisted A person in a Private circle can choose to let the server help for their own data only. Their phone then gives the server a readable copy. This restores server features (admin map, server-side trips, Home Assistant) for that person. Everyone else in the circle stays phone-to-phone. Server-assisted by default (when your server owner turns it on) On a server whose owner chose Home (hardware the family owns), people in a Private circle that has server help on are put on the server by default, so maps, history and driving reports work without everyone finding a setting. It works like this: When you next open the app, your own phone signs "use the server" for you. It is the same signature as tapping Use the server, and it shows in the circle's key log. The server cannot do it for you. You see a notice: Your circle uses the server so maps, history and driving reports work. Tap to keep your data on your phone. Keep on my phone switches you off at once and asks the server to delete what it holds of yours. If you ever chose yourself, in either direction, it is never changed. Opting out stays opted out. From then on the server can read your location, trips and driving data (the server owner and anyone who backs up or steals the server can too). Anything it stored stays until you delete it; backups cannot be deleted. Not done for you: circles that require server processing (you are asked to consent), child accounts, and servers set to Cloud (the app asks you instead). Who decides what The circle admin decides whether server help exists at all for the circle, and the default for new people. Each person decides for themselves, on their own phone. An admin cannot switch you on. (If your server owner chose auto-apply, your own phone does it when you open the app, and you can undo it with one tap.) You can opt out at any time: the server stops receiving new data and the app can delete copies the server already holds. If you are also in a Normal circle, that circle still sends your position to the server. Opting out applies per Private circle, and the screen tells you. What opting out does not hide That you are using the app and roughly when (the server sees that data was uploaded, its size and time). Anything already copied before you opted out, and old backups. Other members: a member who holds the circle key can read what the circle shares. Only add people you trust. Chat, sharing links and SOS Chat is stored readable on the server (see Chat). Share links are for anyone with the link, until they expire. SOS messages work in every mode; see Safety. How to choose Server run by you at home and you want every feature: Normal, or Private with server help on a home server (Deployment profile). Server rented from a hosting company, or someone in the family needs real privacy: Private circle, accept the battery cost. Technical background: Privacy processing design and Operator privacy controls. Which should I pick? Normal (recommended). Your server keeps locations so maps, history and driving reports just work. Private. Only phones can read locations; the server keeps nothing readable. Inside a Private circle each person then chooses Use the server (recommended) (reports, history and maps work for you) or Keep on my phone (shared privately, encrypted from phone to phone; no reports unless you turn on phone reports, which uses more battery). Nobody can choose for you, and you can change your mind any time. If a Private circle shows people missing because their app is old, a circle admin can switch the circle to normal mode so everyone shows up again. The server then keeps readable locations for that circle.

docs.title: Safety: SOS, check-ins and pausing
docs.summary: Orbitly tells your people. It never calls emergency services. If someone is in danger, call your local emergency number first.
docs.text: Safety: SOS, check-ins and pausing Orbitly tells your people. It never calls emergency services. If someone is in danger, call your local emergency number first. SOS Press the SOS button (hold to arm it discreetly). Your circle gets a notification with your last position. If your server admin set up text messages, your own emergency contacts get one too, with a temporary link and no raw coordinates. Every SOS can be tried safely with Practice SOS. No connection to the server? The SOS is kept on your phone, the screen says SOS not sent yet and it is sent as soon as possible; you can also text your emergency contacts from your own messages app. See When the server is down. "I'm here" check-ins Tell chosen people where you are with one tap. A check-in is an explicit act, so it works even while you have paused sharing. Pause sharing Need a break? Pause sharing for an hour, until tomorrow morning or a custom time. Others see "Paused", not your position. The pause ends by itself. Your phone keeps your own history; SOS always shares. More: Safety alerts, Check-ins and temporary sharing.

docs.title: Sharing links
docs.summary: Want a friend or a babysitter to follow you for an evening, without installing anything? Create a share link.
docs.text: Sharing links Want a friend or a babysitter to follow you for an evening, without installing anything? Create a share link. 1. In the app open Sharing and choose Share a link. 2. Pick how long (from a minute up to three days) and add a label. 3. Send the link. Anyone who opens it sees your live position on a small web page: your name, a dot on the map and battery. No history, no account. Stop it at any time from the same screen; the link stops working at once. Links expire on their own. Treat a link like a house key you lent out: anyone who has it can follow you until it ends. Server admins can list and revoke all links on the admin web Sharing page. Technical details: Share links.

docs.title: Removing a member, devices and lost phones
docs.summary: Remove someone from a circle, sign out a lost or replaced phone, and what each person can do with their own devices.

headings.text: Remove a person from a circle

docs.text: Removing a member, devices and lost phones Remove someone from a circle, sign out a lost or replaced phone, and what each person can do with their own devices. Remove a person from a circle Circle admins: open the circle, tap the person, choose Remove. They lose the map, chat and photos immediately. In a Private circle the circle key is renewed so a removed person's phone cannot read anything new. Someone left or changed phone Ask them to sign in on the new phone. For a Private circle the new phone must be approved by one of their other devices, or recovered with their recovery key. Remove the old phone from Settings, Security, Active sessions. Lost or stolen phone 1. Sign in on another device and open Security, Active sessions; sign the lost phone out. Change your password. 2. Ask your server admin to revoke the session on the admin web Audit and sessions page if you cannot. 3. Turn on two-step sign-in so a stolen password alone is not enough. 4. If the phone held a Private circle key, a circle admin should remove and re-add you so the key is renewed. Leaving for good Settings, Delete my account removes your account and data; Download my data exports a copy first.

docs.title: Battery, permissions and keeping tracking alive
docs.summary: For the map to stay current, Android and iOS must let Orbitly run in the background.
docs.text: Battery, permissions and keeping tracking alive For the map to stay current, Android and iOS must let Orbitly run in the background. 1. Allow location "All the time" (not "While using"). 2. Allow notifications and, on Android, "Physical activity" for driving. 3. Android: set battery for Orbitly to Unrestricted or Don't optimize. Samsung, Xiaomi and Huawei phones have an extra "sleeping apps" list; remove Orbitly from it. 4. Install ntfy (or accept the app's built-in channel) so alerts arrive when the app is closed: Notifications. What costs battery Normal use is light. Private circles and driving detection do their calculations on the phone. You may see higher battery and CPU use while driving or after a long offline period. The app warns you before you turn this on. Poor signal, and a "live boost" while someone watches you, use more. Self-test Settings, Phone health (self-test) checks permissions, battery exemptions and connectivity, and the server can warn the circle when a phone goes silent. See Reliability.

docs.title: Orbitly on older phones
docs.summary: How Orbitly adjusts itself to phones with little memory, and which download file to choose.

headings.text: If the app feels slow or gets closed in the background

docs.text: Orbitly on older phones How Orbitly adjusts itself to phones with little memory, and which download file to choose. Orbitly checks how much memory your phone has when it starts and adjusts itself. You do not have to set anything. Your phone What changes Under 4 GB of memory (many phones sold as 2 GB or 3 GB) Lite. The app keeps a shorter recent trail on the phone, loads updates in smaller steps, draws the map with a smaller picture cache and fewer soft shadows, and never does heavy report calculations on the phone itself. 4 GB up to under 6 GB Standard. Everything works; caches are moderate. 6 GB or more Full. Everything works with the largest caches. Nothing you can see is switched off. Older days of history are loaded from the server when you open them instead of being kept on the phone. In a Private circle the server cannot read your history, so those phones keep the last 500 points per person (Lite) instead of 6000. Which file should I install? orbitly-<version>.apk works on every phone. Use this if you are unsure. orbitly-<version>-arm64-v8a.apk is about 40 percent smaller and fits almost every phone made since 2017 with a 64-bit system. orbitly-<version>-armeabi-v7a.apk is for older phones with a 32-bit system. Many 2 GB phones are of this kind. The invite page and the server's download link give you the file that works on every phone. If the app feels slow or gets closed in the background 1. Close apps you are not using. 2. Keep Orbitly set to Unrestricted battery use (see Battery and permissions). Phones with little memory close background apps sooner; this setting asks the phone to keep Orbitly. 3. Restart the phone once if it has been on for weeks. 4. Open Settings, Diagnostics and send the report if it still struggles.

docs.title: When the server is down
docs.summary: What Orbitly shows and keeps for you when your server cannot be reached, and what is sent once it is back.

headings.text: What you cannot see or do until it is back

docs.text: When the server is down What Orbitly shows and keeps for you when your server cannot be reached, and what is sent once it is back. Orbitly keeps working when your server cannot be reached (a restart, an update, a home internet outage, or a phone with no signal). The phone remembers what it last knew and keeps what you do until the server answers again. A small bar at the top of the map tells you what is going on: Server unreachable. Showing last known. Will sync when it is back. The app tries again by itself, a little less often the longer it takes (so it does not drain your battery). Tap Try again to check right now. Syncing… The server is back and things that were waiting are being sent. Up to date Everything has been sent. The bar then goes away. What you still see Everyone's last known position, with how long ago it was ("last seen 3 hours ago"). In Private circles too. Your circles, saved places, the latest chat messages, your check-in notifications and the trips you have already opened. What you can still do Write chat messages. They show "waiting to send", are kept on the phone (even if you close the app or restart the phone) and are sent in order, once, when the server is back. Check in or send a Help alert: it says "Not sent yet" and goes out by itself later. SOS. If the server cannot be reached, the screen says SOS not sent yet. It is kept and retried at once when there is a connection. Meanwhile you can tap Text my emergency contacts (opens your own messages app with your contacts and your last position, you press send, it uses your normal phone plan and does not need Orbitly) or call emergency services. If you are already safe, tap I'm safe, cancel this SOS. Your phone keeps recording your own position. When the server is back it is sent in order, so your history has no gap (up to about 12 hours of positions in a normal circle). What you cannot see or do until it is back New movement of other people. Their phones can only reach you through the server. Photo messages, creating or editing a place in a normal circle, joining a circle with a code, signing in with a password, adding a device. You stay signed in. A network problem never signs you out; only the server saying your login is no longer valid does. How many updates are waiting Settings, Help, Diagnostics shows Updates waiting (positions, messages, check-ins) and a Send now button. More for administrators: design notes.

docs.title: Orbitly on your watch (Wear OS and Apple Watch)
docs.summary: See your people, send "I'm OK" or SOS and reply to chat from a Wear OS or Apple watch, with your phone doing the work. The next sections are about Wear OS; the Apple Watch section is at the end.

headings.text: What you can do on the watch

docs.text: Orbitly on your watch (Wear OS and Apple Watch) See your people, send "I'm OK" or SOS and reply to chat from a Wear OS or Apple watch, with your phone doing the work. The next sections are about Wear OS; the Apple Watch section is at the end. Orbitly has a watch app for Wear OS 3 and newer: Samsung Galaxy Watch 4 and later, Google Pixel Watch, and other Wear OS 3+ watches. Older Samsung watches that run Tizen (Galaxy Watch 3 and earlier, Galaxy Watch Active, Gear) are a different system and are not supported. The watch is a companion to your phone. It shows your people and lets you send an "I'm OK", an SOS or a quick reply from your wrist. Your phone does the real work, so Orbitly must be installed and signed in on the phone that the watch is paired with. What you can do on the watch People: who is where ("At Home", "Driving 42 mph", "2 min ago"), battery, and for each person the place, how old the position is, and Open on phone. Direction: a simple arrow and distance to a person from where your watch is (if you allow location for Orbitly on the watch). There is no map on the watch. I'm OK: tells your circle you are fine, with where you are. SOS: press and hold, then you have 5 seconds to cancel. Your family is told. Emergency services are not called. If the watch says it could not send, call emergency services yourself. Pause or resume sharing, quick replies to your circle's chat (a fixed list such as "On my way"), unread count, and alerts. A tile with the people nearest to you and a watch face complication (nearest person, unread messages or "Sharing paused"). If the phone is out of reach, the watch shows the last information it got, says how old it is and says "Phone not connected". Install From Google Play (when available): open Orbitly in the Play Store on your phone, choose the watch under "Install on more devices", or search for Orbitly in the Play Store on the watch. From the release file (no Play Store): 1. Download orbitly-wear-<version>.apk from the same release as the phone app. Check it against SHA256SUMS-wear.txt. 2. On the watch: Settings, About watch, Software, tap Software version 7 times to unlock Developer options. In Developer options turn on ADB debugging and Debug over Wi-Fi (watch and computer on the same Wi-Fi). Note the IP address and port shown. 3. On the computer: adb connect <watch-ip>:<port>, then adb -s <watch-ip>:<port> install orbitly-wear-<version>.apk. (Some watches ask you to pair with a code first: adb pair <ip>:<pair-port>.) 4. Open Orbitly on the phone first, then open the watch app. The watch app and the phone app must be the same release family and signed by the same key. Android only connects them when they match, which is also what keeps other apps out. Mixing a Play-Store phone app with a release-file watch app (or the other way round) will not connect. On the phone, Settings, Watch shows if a watch is connected and has two switches: "Send to my watch" and "Show Private circles". How it works Your phone keeps your sign-in and your encryption keys. It sends the watch a short summary (names, last places, battery, alerts) over the normal Bluetooth/Wi-Fi link between a phone and its paired Wear OS watch. When you press something on the watch, the watch asks the phone, and the phone does it. The watch app has no internet permission and never talks to your server. Because the phone does the work: the watch is only as up to date as the phone (when the phone is off or far away, the watch shows old data and cannot send anything); the Orbitly app has to be running on the phone for buttons on the watch to work. Orbitly keeps running on its own for location sharing, but if you swiped it away or Android stopped it, the watch tells you to open Orbitly on the phone. Privacy Normal circles: the watch shows the same things the phone shows. Private circles: the positions are readable only on phones. To show them on the watch, the phone sends them already readable to your watch. They travel only between your phone and your paired watch and are never sent to the server by this feature. They are, however, readable on the watch itself and are handled by Google Play services on both devices. If you do not want that, turn off Settings, Watch, Show Private circles: those people then do not appear on the watch at all. The watch keeps only the last summary. Signing out of Orbitly on the phone, or turning off "Send to my watch", removes it from the watch. Anyone who holds your unlocked watch can see that summary and press "I'm OK" or SOS, the same as someone holding your unlocked phone. Use a watch screen lock. Troubleshooting "Open Orbitly on your phone": the phone has not sent anything yet, or you are signed out there. Open the app on the phone. "Phone not connected": the watch is out of Bluetooth range or its link is off. The data shown is old; its age is next to the message. Nothing shows in Settings, Watch: the phone needs Google Play services and a paired Wear OS watch (through the Google "Wear OS" app). Samsung phones: allow Orbitly to run in the background (Battery and permissions). Apple Watch Orbitly has an Apple Watch app for watchOS 9 or newer that does the same as the Wear OS app, with your iPhone doing the work. This app is new and has not yet been tried on a real watch. Install. Install Orbitly on your iPhone and sign in. Open the Watch app on the iPhone, find Orbitly and switch on Show App on Apple Watch (it also installs by itself when automatic app install is on). In Orbitly on the iPhone, Settings, Watch shows whether the watch is found and has the same two switches as on Android. What you can do. People (name, where, how long ago, battery), a distance and direction arrow (north is at the top; it does not turn with your wrist), SOS (press and hold, 5 second countdown, Cancel), I'm OK, pause or resume sharing, quick replies with an unread count, and alerts. If the iPhone cannot be reached the watch says "iPhone not reachable" and shows the age of what it has. An SOS that could not be sent is shown as not sent: call emergency services yourself. Orbitly never calls them. Privacy. The watch never has your sign-in or keys. The iPhone sends it names, places and battery directly (not through the server). For a Private circle the iPhone sends the readable version the same way; turn off Settings, Watch, Show Private circles to leave those people out. Signing out, or switching "Send to my watch" off, removes the data from the watch; if the watch is out of reach at that moment the removal is done as soon as it is back. Installed from the unsigned file (sideloading). The unsigned orbitly-<version>-unsigned.ipa contains the watch app. The tool you re-sign with must sign the watch app too; some tools only sign the main app. If Orbitly does not show up in the Watch app on the iPhone, sign again with a tool that supports watch apps, or install without the watch part. A free Apple ID limits how many app identifiers you can create per week and a watch app needs one more; apps signed with a free Apple ID expire after 7 days. Technical background: Watch apps (design) and Apple Watch app.

categories.title: Running your server
categories.description: Install, update, back up and look after your own server.

docs.title: Install the server with Docker Compose
docs.summary: This guide takes you from an empty machine to a running Orbitly server. You need about 20 minutes and a computer that stays on: a small home server, a NAS that runs Docker, a Raspberry Pi 4 or newer…
docs.text: Install the server with Docker Compose This guide takes you from an empty machine to a running Orbitly server. You need about 20 minutes and a computer that stays on: a small home server, a NAS that runs Docker, a Raspberry Pi 4 or newer, or a rented VPS. Formerly OpenFamily. Orbitly is the new name of OpenFamily. If you already run a server, you do not reinstall: just update. Your folder, database, .env and Docker volumes keep their old openfamily names on purpose, see Naming. What you need A Linux machine (or NAS) with Docker and Docker Compose v2 (docker compose version prints a version). 1 GB of free RAM and a few GB of disk. Locations are small. Optional but recommended: a domain name (see HTTPS and your own domain). Step by step 1. Get the code. git clone https://github.com/TheTractorHacker/orbitly.git cd orbitly 2. Create your settings. The setup script writes a .env file with random passwords and asks two questions: your address and the admin email. ./scripts/setup.sh Answer :80 for a first test on your own network, or your domain name (for example family.example.com) for the internet. It never overwrites an existing .env. The admin password is shown once; save it in a password manager. 3. Start the server. docker compose up -d --build The first build takes a few minutes. The documentation you are reading is built into the server image, so it is available offline afterwards. 4. Check that it is alive. curl http://localhost:8080/healthz {"status":"ok"} 5. Open the admin web at http://localhost:8080/admin/ (or your domain plus /admin/) and sign in with the admin email and password from step 2. Continue with First run. Where things live What Where Settings .env next to docker-compose.yml Family data Docker volume pgdata (Postgres) Backups ./backups/ after you run scripts/backup.sh Logs docker compose logs -f api Stop, start, remove docker compose stop # stop, keep data docker compose up -d # start again docker compose down # remove containers, KEEP data docker compose down -v # DANGER: also deletes the database Next: First run, Backups, Updates. The full checklist for internet-facing servers is in Self-hosting.

docs.title: First run: your first sign-in and your first circle
docs.summary: Your first sign-in to the admin web: registration is closed, turn on two-step sign-in, create the first circle and check the settings that matter.

headings.text: What a server admin can and cannot see
The admin web at a glance

docs.text: First run: your first sign-in and your first circle Your first sign-in to the admin web: registration is closed, turn on two-step sign-in, create the first circle and check the settings that matter. 1. Open the admin web and sign in. Because you set an admin email during setup, open registration is closed: new people need an invite code. 2. Turn on two-step sign-in for your admin account in the app (Settings, Security). You can require this for every admin with REQUIREADMINMFA=true. 3. In the app: create your account with the same email, then create a circle and invite your family. 4. In the admin web look at Families, Users and System: 5. Open Settings and check: Deployment profile: home or cloud (explained here). Backups: see Backups. App versions: see App versions. 6. Give your family the install instructions: Installing on Android. What a server admin can and cannot see By default a server admin sees accounts, circles, devices and audit logs, but not where anyone is (ADMINLOCATIONACCESS=false). If you turn it on, every look is written to an audit log the circle can read. Private circles are unreadable by the server unless members opt in. See Privacy modes explained and Operator privacy controls. The admin web at a glance Page Use it to Dashboard Live map of everyone you are allowed to see Families, Users Accounts, roles, invites, password reset codes Places, Circles, Sharing Saved places, circle settings, share links Activity, Alerts, Audit What happened, SOS and check-ins, who looked at what Fleet Which phones are reporting and which have gone silent System Version, database, warnings, last backup Builds Download the Android app from your own server Documents These guides, offline, plus what is new in your server version Settings Map style, SMS, domain, integrations, app versions

docs.title: HTTPS, reverse proxies and your own domain
docs.summary: Phones should always talk to your server over HTTPS. There are two ways to get it.

headings.text: Option B: your own reverse proxy

docs.text: HTTPS, reverse proxies and your own domain Phones should always talk to your server over HTTPS. There are two ways to get it. Option A: the built-in Caddy (easiest) 1. Point a DNS name at your server and forward ports 80 and 443 (custom domain guide has the DNS table). 2. In .env set SITEADDRESS=family.example.com and COMPOSEPROFILES=proxy. 3. docker compose up -d. Caddy gets and renews a Let's Encrypt certificate. 4. In the admin web open Settings, Custom domain: it checks DNS and HTTPS for you. Option B: your own reverse proxy Already running nginx, Traefik or Nginx Proxy Manager? Leave proxy off and point it at 127.0.0.1:8080. Keep TLSBEHINDPROXY=true. Pass WebSocket upgrades (/ws/stream, /api/admin/ws) and do not buffer /push/stream (server-sent events). Home network without a domain Use the server's LAN address (http://192.168.1.20:8080) while at home. Phones leaving home will not reach it: use a domain, or a VPN such as WireGuard or Tailscale. Plain http on the internet is not supported. Details and troubleshooting: Custom domains and Self-hosting.

docs.title: Updating the server
docs.summary: Updating is a script on the server, never a button on the web. That keeps the web page from holding powers over your machine.
docs.text: Updating the server Updating is a script on the server, never a button on the web. That keeps the web page from holding powers over your machine. ./scripts/upgrade.sh It makes a backup, pulls the new version, rebuilds, waits until /healthz is healthy and rolls back to the previous version if it is not. Run it from the server's Orbitly folder (it may still be called openfamily) with no uncommitted changes. Before you update Read What is new (also on the admin Documents page). Check App versions: after the update the server supports the last five app versions. People on older apps see "Update required". Make sure you have a recent backup. After you update Admin web, System: confirm the version and a healthy database. Admin web, Settings, App versions: see who needs a nudge, and copy the ready-made message. The Documents page now shows the notes for the new version. Updating the phones Family members update the app via Obtainium or the store. The server keeps working for the last five minor versions, so nobody has to update on the same day. See API compatibility. Watch app. Each release can also carry orbitly-wear-<version>.apk (and an .aab), the Wear OS watch app, built by a separate workflow (wear.yml) and attached to the same release once the phone build has created it. The watch app needs nothing on your server; it only talks to the phone it is paired with. Update it with the phone app, see Orbitly on your watch. The server's APK download never serves the watch file. Something went wrong upgrade.sh prints how to restore the pre-upgrade backup. See Backup and restore and Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Backups and restore
docs.summary: Your family's data lives in one Docker volume. Back it up before you need it.
docs.text: Backups and restore Your family's data lives in one Docker volume. Back it up before you need it. Quick backup ./scripts/backup.sh # writes ./backups/openfamily-<time>.dump ./scripts/verify-backup.sh backups/<file>.dump # restore into a scratch database and compare Schedule it daily with cron and copy backups/ off the machine (another disk, a cloud bucket). The admin System page warns when the last backup is missing or older than 48 hours. Scheduled, encrypted off-site backups Turn on the backup compose profile and enter an S3-compatible bucket (AWS, Backblaze B2, Wasabi, Cloudflare R2, MinIO) in Settings, Backups. Copies are encrypted on your server before upload and old ones are removed by a retention rule. Back up now and Test S3 buttons are on the same card. Restore ./scripts/restore.sh backups/<file>.dump # DESTRUCTIVE: asks you to type RESTORE Do not forget Back up your .env (it holds the secrets that unlock sealed settings). Turn on disk encryption on the machine. Keep the Android signing key safe if you build your own app. Everything in depth, including recovery objectives and snapshots: Backup and restore.

docs.title: Notifications: push, SMS and Apple push
docs.summary: Alerts (SOS, arrivals, check-ins, chat) reach phones in three ways. You only need the first for Android.

headings.text: Android: built in (nothing to set up)

docs.text: Notifications: push, SMS and Apple push Alerts (SOS, arrivals, check-ins, chat) reach phones in three ways. You only need the first for Android. Android: built in (nothing to set up) The app keeps a connection to your server and shows alerts as notifications. Make sure the app is allowed to run in the background (Battery and permissions). If phones sleep deeply, add ntfy (UnifiedPush): COMPOSEPROFILES=proxy,push PUSHADDRESS=push.example.com NTFYBASEURL=https://push.example.com CADDYFILE=Caddyfile.with-push Install the ntfy app on each phone. Details: Push notifications. iPhone: Apple push (APNs) Needs an Apple developer account and a .p8 key. Set the key id, team id and bundle id in .env as described in Push notifications and iOS release. SMS for SOS (optional) If you add an SMS provider (Twilio, Telnyx, Plivo or Amazon SNS), an SOS also texts the sender's own emergency contacts, with a temporary link and no coordinates. Set the provider in .env or in Settings, SMS in the admin web, and set PUBLICBASEURL=https://family.example.com. Messages never claim emergency services were called. Register your number where your country requires it. Details: SMS providers and Safety. Push messages never contain a location, and by default not the person's name or the message text either (VERBOSEPUSH=true changes that).

docs.title: Integrations: Home Assistant and Dawarich
docs.summary: Connect Orbitly to Home Assistant (who is home, arrival automations) or Dawarich (a location history service you run) using a token you control.
docs.text: Integrations: Home Assistant and Dawarich Connect Orbitly to Home Assistant (who is home, arrival automations) or Dawarich (a location history service you run) using a token you control. Home Assistant Show who is home, trigger automations when someone arrives, or light a lamp when a child leaves school. 1. In the app (Settings, Integrations) create a Home Assistant token. It is read-only, scoped to the circles you choose, and shown once. 2. Install the Orbitly custom component in Home Assistant and paste the server address and token. 3. Optionally enable signed webhooks for events. Admins can see tokens and revoke them on the admin web. Full guide with examples: Home Assistant. Dawarich Dawarich is a self-hosted location history viewer. Orbitly can push points to it, one way. Configure it under Settings, Dawarich: address, API key, per-member mapping. Deleting points in Orbitly does not delete them in Dawarich. In Private circles the Dawarich bridge is an approved device that members must allow. Design notes: Dawarich. Privacy of integrations Both only receive what the circle's privacy mode allows. A person who keeps their data phone-only is not sent to either.

docs.title: Deployment profile: home or cloud
docs.summary: Tell the server whether it runs on hardware your family owns (a box at home) or on rented hardware (a VPS or hosting company). This changes the advice and the defaults the apps show; it never turns…

headings.text: The server's own key (no extra container)
Members are on the server by default (auto-apply)

docs.text: Deployment profile: home or cloud Tell the server whether it runs on hardware your family owns (a box at home) or on rented hardware (a VPS or hosting company). This changes the advice and the defaults the apps show; it never turns anything on for anyone. Profile Meaning Effect Home You own the machine and the room it sits in. The apps may suggest server help for people who want the full feature set. Cloud Someone else runs the machine or the network. The apps suggest phone-to-phone privacy and warn before sharing readable copies with the server. Not chosen Treated as Cloud, the careful side. Every circle admin and member still chooses on their own phone. Nobody, including you, can consent for another person. Set it in the admin web under Settings, Deployment profile, or seed a fresh install with DEPLOYMENTPROFILE=home in .env. The choice in Settings wins. Related: Privacy modes explained, Privacy processing design. The server's own key (no extra container) From the release that adds it, the server is its own circle device. It creates the key itself on first start (serverdevice volume, /data/server-device), you approve it once on a phone, and the setup card on Settings turns into a green Server is processing. Nothing to type and no extra container. See Server setup for the three steps, the accepted trade-off (the key lives on the server's own disk) and what a cloud server should do (OPENFAMILYDATAKEY encrypts the key file at rest). Defaults for new members. Server processing is suggested when the profile is Home or the admin chose the server as the default; Cloud and not chosen keep the suggestion on "Keep on my phone" until you decide. Whatever is suggested, the person still taps for themselves. Members are on the server by default (auto-apply) The member default (API GET/PUT /api/admin/settings/member-defaults; the admin web page for it may arrive in a later release): Setting Home profile (default) Cloud or not chosen (default) Default lane Server Phone Auto-apply On Off (the app only asks) With auto-apply on, a member of a Private circle that has server help on, an approved server key and no earlier choice gets "use the server" signed by their own phone the next time they open the app. It is the same signature as tapping the button, it appears in the circle's key log, and the member sees a notice with a one-tap Keep on my phone (which also deletes the copies the server holds of them). Nobody who ever chose is changed, and an opt-out is permanent. Not auto-applied: circles that require server processing, child accounts, old apps (they apply after updating) and phones that are not online. The background service cannot sign, so a member who never opens the app is not switched. This is your policy, not each person's consent in advance: say so to your family. After it applies, the server (and you, as its operator) can read that member's location, trips and driving data, and backups include them. Who is not on yet. GET /api/admin/members-not-on-server (and the circle's processing screen for circle admins) lists members whose own lane is not Server: nochoice (covered at their next app open), phone (their choice; nobody can change it for them) and needsupdate (old app). remindtext is a message you can send. Circles that are already Private Open the app as the circle admin: a card says Let the server do the processing (recommended). One flow approves the server, turns server help on and signs your own choice. Every other member then opens the app and taps Use the server. For members on an old app, the sheet gives a Message to send and the circle shows "needs update". If people cannot send at all, Switch this circle to normal mode makes the server keep everyone's locations again: the encrypted copies and key copies the server held for that circle are deleted, phone-only places and history stay on those phones, and every member is told. Availability: the deployment profile arrives with the release that adds it; see the changelog for your version.

docs.title: App versions and what your server supports
docs.summary: People update phones slowly. The server therefore keeps working for the last five minor versions of the app (for example 0.18 to 0.22). Open the admin web Settings, App versions to see:
docs.text: App versions and what your server supports People update phones slowly. The server therefore keeps working for the last five minor versions of the app (for example 0.18 to 0.22). Open the admin web Settings, App versions to see: The server version and what is new in it (also in Documents). The supported window and the oldest version that is fully supported.
