Which app versions are in use, per person and per platform. For anyone outside the window: what that person will experience, and a ready message you can copy and send. What people see Their app is They experience Inside the window Everything works. 2 or more versions behind the newest Works. A small dismissible "newer version available" note. Older than the window An "Update required" banner; circles needing newer features say "update the app to open this private circle". If you switch on enforcement, location uploads from that app are refused until it updates. Not reporting a version Old app or script; never blocked. Settings Minimum supported version (override) lets you widen or narrow the window. Refuse location uploads from apps below the minimum is off by default. Turn it on only if you must retire an old version. The same facts are available to the app at GET /compat. The policy in full: API compatibility.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.summary: A quick checklist for the server admin. The full hub with every topic is Troubleshooting.

headings.text: After an update something is off

docs.text: Troubleshooting A quick checklist for the server admin. The full hub with every topic is Troubleshooting. Start with docker compose ps (all services "healthy"/"running"), curl http://localhost:8080/healthz and docker compose logs --tail 100 api. The admin System page lists recent warnings and errors. Nobody shows on the map Work down this list; most cases end at step 2 or 3. 1. Is the server reachable from the phone? Open the server address in the phone's browser. If it fails, fix DNS, ports 80/443 or the VPN first (HTTPS and domain). 2. Is the phone allowed to report? Location "All the time", battery Unrestricted (Battery and permissions). The admin Fleet page shows the last time each phone reported. 3. Is the person sharing? Check the circle's "Share my location" and that they have not paused sharing. 4. Do you use a Private circle? The admin web cannot show a Private circle unless you are a member who approved the browser. Positions are sealed (Privacy modes explained). 5. Can an admin look at members? The admin map is empty by design unless ADMINLOCATIONACCESS=true. 6. Is the app too old? Check App versions: with enforcement on, an unsupported app's uploads are refused. 7. Map tiles missing but people listed? The tile provider is unreachable; see "Map tiles" in Self-hosting. A fuller step-by-step: No locations. Alerts do not arrive See Notifications and Push. Check ntfy is installed, and that Android is not putting the app to sleep. Admin web says "Access denied" Only platform admins see admin pages. If REQUIREADMINMFA=true, turn on two-step sign-in in the app, sign out and in again. The server will not start docker compose run --rm api validate-config prints what is wrong without revealing secrets. Common causes: JWTSECRET or POSTGRESPASSWORD unset, a database TLS setting (Self-hosting). After an update something is off ./scripts/upgrade.sh rolls back on failure. Otherwise restore the backups/pre-upgrade-.dump (Backups). Still stuck Open an issue at https://github.com/TheTractorHacker/orbitly/issues with the server version (admin web footer) and the last lines of docker compose logs api. Remove addresses and secrets first.

docs.title: "Nobody's location shows" in a Private circle
docs.summary: This page explains, in plain words, why a family can open Orbitly, be in a Private (end-to-end encrypted) circle, and see no one, and what the app now does about it.

headings.text: What happened to the Foley family
The causes we found in the code
Things we checked and found fine
One thing we could not prove from the code

docs.text: "Nobody's location shows" in a Private circle This page explains, in plain words, why a family can open Orbitly, be in a Private (end-to-end encrypted) circle, and see no one, and what the app now does about it. What happened to the Foley family Their circle went private on 6 November 2026. Both people had app 0.21.1 on Android. Afterwards the server held 807 encrypted updates, all from one phone. The other phone had never sent a single one. Neither phone showed the other. There were several separate problems. Any one of them gives an empty map, and the app used to say only "No location yet" for all of them. The causes we found in the code 1. A phone that was given the circle key never picked it up. When a circle turns private, an admin's phone puts a locked copy of the circle key on the server for every member's phone. That copy is useless until the member's phone downloads and opens it. The only places that did this were the Encryption keys screens and a retry that only ran if the phone already had something to send. A phone without the key has nothing to send, so nothing ever triggered the download. It could neither send its own position nor read anyone else's. This is the most likely reason one phone never sent a single update. Fix: every time the app opens, resumes, or a position is taken without the key, the phone fetches its key first and then sends the positions that were waiting for it. 2. The background part of the app could be out of date about the circle. The background location service lives for days. It learned "this circle is private" once, and kept that answer. If it had learned it while the circle was still normal, it kept sending ordinary (readable) positions. The server refuses those for a private circle (error 409), so they were thrown away. Fix: the background service re-reads the circle settings on every position. 3. Updates could be thrown away for a temporary reason. A phone that was offline for a while, or whose login was being renewed, counted each failed attempt against its waiting updates and dropped them after 20 attempts. A refusal from the server for a lasting reason (for example "this phone is not approved") dropped the updates silently. Fix: being offline or renewing a login never uses up an update. A lasting refusal is remembered and shown on the "Why can't I see everyone?" screen. 4. Nothing was sent when the circle turned private, or when the app was opened. The first view stayed empty until the next GPS position arrived (can be many minutes for a phone sitting still). Fix: when a circle turns private, and when the app is opened after a quiet spell, the phone immediately sends its last known position (with its original time, so it never pretends to be newer). 5. Admin phones only shared keys when someone opened a screen. A member who joined, or got a new phone, waited until an admin happened to open Encryption keys. Fix: an admin's phone now does the automatic, safe part of that whenever the app opens. Anything that needs a person's decision still asks. 6. Not knowing why. The app showed "No location yet" for a missing key, an old app, a switched-off phone, paused sharing and a bug alike. Fix: see "What you will see now". Things we checked and found fine Server rules for ordinary circles. Since 0.22 the server hides the stored position of a member who keeps their data on their phone. We tested that a member of a normal circle, a member of a private circle who lets the server help (server lane), and a member who is in both a private and a normal circle all still appear on the family list and on the live connection. Only a phone-only member of a private circle has no server position, which is the point of the feature. Expiry and paging. Live updates are kept 48 hours; the reading phone pages through everything after its saved place, oldest first, and never skips ahead past an update it could not open yet (those wait and are retried once the key arrives). No readable fallback. A private circle never sends a readable position as a fallback; a phone without the key keeps the position on the phone until it can seal it. One thing we could not prove from the code Blake's updates stopped around 13:51 UTC. The code explains several ways that can happen (the phone went offline and used up its 20 attempts, the login was being renewed, the phone was switched off, the operating system stopped the background service). The server cannot tell these apart. Items 2 and 3 above remove the code-side ones. If it happens again, the new screen shows whether the phone is queuing, refused, or silent. What you will see now People list, member card and map: instead of "No location yet", the reason, for example "Kinsley hasn't sent an encrypted update since 9:02 am (their phone may be off or the app closed)" "Kinsley's phone has not received the circle key yet" "Kinsley needs to update the app (v0.15.0 is too old)" "Location sharing paused by Kinsley" A banner when everyone is silent: "You are in private mode and nobody has sent an update." Circle settings, "Why can't I see everyone?" shows each member's reason, what this phone has done (has the key, updates waiting, updates refused), and a Fix this circle button. It fetches the key, shares waiting keys (admin), seals waiting positions, sends your last position, uploads, and downloads what others sent, then lists what it did. Admin web, Private circles, Delivery table shows the same per-member reasons. All of this uses only what the server already knows (who holds a key copy, when an encrypted update last arrived to the minute, the app version, the sharing switch). GET /circles/{id}/delivery never returns or touches a position. What to do, in order 1. Open Orbitly on both phones and keep them open for a minute. Updates are sent immediately on open. 2. Tap Circle settings, Why can't I see everyone?, Fix this circle on the phone that sees nobody. 3. If someone is on an old app, update it. Private circles need 0.16 or newer, and per-member privacy settings need 0.22. 4. If a member's phone says "waiting for an admin to approve", an admin opens Settings, Security, Encryption keys for the circle. 5. Phones that are off, or where the system has stopped the app in the background, can only send once the app is opened again. On Android, allow Orbitly to run in the background and exclude it from battery saving.

docs.title: Self-hosting Orbitly
docs.summary: Production checklist for operators. The README Quick start is enough for a laptop. Use this before you invite a family onto a VPS or NAS that is reachable from the internet.
docs.text: Self-hosting Orbitly Production checklist for operators. The README Quick start is enough for a laptop. Use this before you invite a family onto a VPS or NAS that is reachable from the internet. Before docker compose up ./scripts/setup.sh This writes .env (never overwriting an existing one) with a random POSTGRESPASSWORD, JWTSECRET and first-admin password, and asks for your SITEADDRESS and PLATFORMADMINEMAIL. Compose refuses to start if POSTGRESPASSWORD or JWTSECRET is unset; there are no default passwords. Doing it by hand instead: copy .env.example to .env and set 1. JWTSECRET (at least 32 random bytes, openssl rand -hex 32) and POSTGRESPASSWORD (use a hex/alphanumeric value; it is embedded in a URL). 2. SITEADDRESS=orbitly.example.com and COMPOSEPROFILES=proxy so Caddy requests a certificate. 3. APPENV=production and DBSSLDISABLEOK=true (see Database TLS below). 4. PLATFORMADMINEMAIL and PLATFORMADMINPASSWORD. This creates the first admin and closes open registration (invite codes required). Optional components (compose profiles) Profile Service Enable when (none) api, postgres Always. The API is published on 127.0.0.1:8080 only. proxy caddy You want HTTPS on a domain without bringing your own reverse proxy. push ntfy You want Android push (UnifiedPush) hosted by you. Enable with COMPOSEPROFILES=proxy,push in .env or docker compose --profile proxy up -d. Without proxy, put your own TLS reverse proxy in front of 127.0.0.1:8080 (the API trusts it because TLSBEHINDPROXY=true). All images are pinned to explicit versions; services drop all Linux capabilities, use no-new-privileges, and have CPU/memory limits (edit deploy.resources.limits in docker-compose.yml for small or large hosts). The Caddyfiles set HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, Referrer-Policy and Permissions-Policy headers (no CSP, to avoid breaking the admin panel). Database TLS APPENV=production makes the API reject sslmode=disable, prefer, allow and a missing sslmode. The bundled Postgres is reachable only on the private Compose network and has no TLS configured, so setup.sh sets DBSSLDISABLEOK=true for production installs. If Postgres runs elsewhere or is published, set DATABASEURL=...?sslmode=verify-full, leave DBSSLDISABLEOK unset, and configure server certificates on Postgres. In APPENV=development (the default) nothing is enforced. Upgrades and backups ./scripts/backup.sh # ./backups/openfamily-<UTC time>.dump (BACKUPKEEP=N prunes) ./scripts/restore.sh backups/<file>.dump # DESTRUCTIVE; asks you to type RESTORE ./scripts/verify-backup.sh backups/<file>.dump # restore into a throwaway container and compare row counts ./scripts/upgrade.sh # backup, pull, rebuild, wait for /healthz, roll back on failure upgrade.sh refuses to run with uncommitted changes, writes backups/pre-upgrade-.dump, runs git pull --ff-only, docker compose up -d build, and polls /healthz (HEALTHTIMEOUT, default 120s). On failure it checks out the previous git ref, rebuilds, and prints the restore.sh command for the pre-upgrade dump, since migrations that already ran are not undone by a code rollback. There is no in-app updater and no Docker socket access. Schedule backup.sh from cron and copy backups/ off the host. Encrypt copies with BACKUPPASSPHRASEFILE; RPO/RTO, volume snapshots and the restore drill are in backup-restore.md. For scheduled backups without host cron, optional S3-compatible off-site copies (AWS S3, Backblaze B2, Wasabi, Cloudflare R2, MinIO), client-side age encryption and retention, enable the backup compose profile; the admin System page then shows the last backup per destination and has a Back up now button. See S3 and scheduled backups. Validate your configuration before starting (non-zero exit on errors; secret values are never printed): docker compose run --rm api validate-config. Step 5 in detail — DNS records, certificate behavior, and troubleshooting — is covered in custom-domain.md. The admin panel's Settings → Custom domain card runs live DNS and HTTPS checks against your setup. Admin panel hardening and health REQUIREADMINMFA=true in .env refuses the admin panel and /api/admin/ to any platform admin who has not turned on two-factor (TOTP). The admin enables it in the app (Settings, Security), then signs out and in again with their code: the panel only accepts sessions that passed a TOTP challenge, so sessions that predate it are refused. No restart is needed. Signing in itself is unchanged. Sign-ins can be listed and revoked on the panel's Audit & sessions page. The System health page shows the release, database migration version and size, recent server warnings and errors, and the last backup. ./scripts/backup.sh records each successful backup in the database; the page flags a backup that is missing or older than 48 hours, so schedule it (for example a daily cron job). Android push (ntfy) Do not publish ntfy on 0.0.0.0:2586. Compose binds loopback only, and the service only exists with the push profile. For phones on the public internet: COMPOSEPROFILES=proxy,push PUSHADDRESS=push.example.com NTFYBASEURL=https://push.example.com CADDYFILE=Caddyfile.with-push Install the ntfy Android app on each phone. UnifiedPush registration is silent; if alerts never arrive, ntfy is usually missing. Map tiles Default street tiles are public OSM; satellite is Esri. Those hosts see the viewport. To use another raster provider (API key goes in the URL): TILEURL=https://tiles.example.com/{z}/{x}/{y}.png?apikey=xxx SATELLITETILEURL= The API returns these on GET /config. The generic APK does not need a rebuild. A key in TILEURL is visible to every phone. Optional SMS Set TWILIO and PUBLICBASEURL=https://orbitly.example.com so SOS messages carry a share link instead of raw coordinates. The same values can be saved on the admin Settings page; a saved row overrides empty env values without restarting. Emergency contacts appear in the app only when SMS is configured. Backups and disk encryption Volume pgdata is the family database. Use ./scripts/backup.sh (above) on a schedule and keep copies off the host. Enable host disk encryption (LUKS, Synology volume encryption, cloud disk encryption). The app does not encrypt rows itself. Keep app/android/upload-keystore.jks (or CI signing secrets) backed up. Losing the keystore forces every phone to uninstall before they can update. Family setup (give this to members) 1. Install the Android APK from the admin Builds page (or the GitHub Release). 2. Enter https://orbitly.example.com and Connect. 3. Create an account (invite code if the server requires one). 4. Allow Always location, notifications, and the battery exemption. 5. Install ntfy so alerts arrive when the app is closed.

docs.title: Custom domains
docs.summary: Serving Orbitly behind a real domain name (for example orbitly.example.com) gives every device automatic HTTPS: Caddy requests and renews a Let's Encrypt certificate for you. No certbot, no manual…

headings.text: Android push on its own subdomain

docs.text: Custom domains Serving Orbitly behind a real domain name (for example orbitly.example.com) gives every device automatic HTTPS: Caddy requests and renews a Let's Encrypt certificate for you. No certbot, no manual renewal. The admin panel (Settings → Custom domain) shows your current setup and runs live DNS and HTTPS checks against it, so you can verify each step below without SSH-ing into the server. 1. Point DNS at the server At your DNS provider, create a record for the name you want: Record Name Value A orbitly.example.com your server's public IPv4 AAAA orbitly.example.com your server's public IPv6 (optional) If your server sits behind a router (home NAS), forward external ports 80 and 443 to it. Port 80 is required even though traffic ends up on 443: Let's Encrypt uses it for the initial challenge and for HTTP→HTTPS redirects. DNS changes can take minutes to hours to propagate. The panel's DNS check tells you when the name resolves. 2. Set the domain in .env In the .env file next to docker-compose.yml: SITEADDRESS=orbitly.example.com ALLOWEDORIGIN=https://orbitly.example.com PUBLICBASEURL=https://orbitly.example.com APPENV=production SITEADDRESS — what Caddy serves; this is what triggers certificate issuance. ALLOWEDORIGIN — must match the origin exactly (scheme included) or app clients will fail CORS. PUBLICBASEURL — used for share links in SMS alerts. 3. Apply and verify docker compose up -d Caddy obtains the certificate on startup (it may take a few seconds). The panel's HTTPS check passes once https://your-domain/healthz answers from the server with a valid certificate. Then point the apps at https://your-domain (Settings → About → Copy server URL in the web panel). Home-network note: some routers do not support NAT loopback, so the server may not be able to reach its own domain even though phones outside the network can. If the HTTPS check fails but everything else works, test from a phone on mobile data before debugging further. Android push on its own subdomain Phones on the public internet need to reach the ntfy push server over TLS. Give it a second name (e.g. push.example.com, an A record at the same IP) and set in .env: PUSHADDRESS=push.example.com NTFYBASEURL=https://push.example.com CADDYFILE=Caddyfile.with-push Keep ntfy bound to loopback only (the Compose default); Caddy is the only public entrypoint. See self-hosting.md for details. Troubleshooting "DNS check fails: does not resolve yet" — the record does not exist or has not propagated. Double-check the name and value at your provider. Certificate errors right after switching — Caddy needs outbound access to Let's Encrypt and inbound port 80 for the challenge. Wait a minute and re-run the checks. App can't connect after the switch — ALLOWEDORIGIN usually doesn't match https://your-domain exactly. Domain changed? Update SITEADDRESS, ALLOWEDORIGIN, PUBLICBASEURL (and the push trio if used) together, then docker compose up -d. All values live in .env, which survives server self-updates.

docs.title: Backup and restore
docs.summary: The family database (Postgres + TimescaleDB, volume pgdata) holds location history, so backups are as sensitive as the live data. Encrypt any copy that leaves the host.

headings.text: Quick start 1: in the admin panel (recommended)
Security review of the credential and encryption path

docs.text: Backup and restore The family database (Postgres + TimescaleDB, volume pgdata) holds location history, so backups are as sensitive as the live data. Encrypt any copy that leaves the host. Scripts Script Purpose scripts/backup.sh [file] pgdump --format=custom of the running postgres service into backups/ (mode 700/600). BACKUPKEEP=N prunes old automatic backups. With BACKUPPASSPHRASEFILE=/path the dump is encrypted (AES-256-CBC, PBKDF2 600k iterations) and written as .dump.enc. scripts/restore.sh <file> [--yes] DESTRUCTIVE. Stops the api, recreates the database, runs timescaledbprerestore(), pgrestore, timescaledbpostrestore(), restarts the api. .enc files need BACKUPPASSPHRASEFILE. scripts/verify-backup.sh <file> Restores the backup into a throwaway TimescaleDB container (the image pinned in docker-compose.yml), never the live database, and prints a row count per table. Exits non-zero if the restore errors, the schema is empty, or counts differ from --expect-counts FILE / --source-container NAME. scripts/restore.sh --from-s3 [latest\NAME] Same restore, but downloads from your S3 bucket first: SHA-256 checked against the manifest, then age-decrypted with BACKUPAGEIDENTITYFILE. --from-local does the same for the backup service's local directory. See S3 and scheduled backups. scripts/verify-backup.sh --from-s3 [latest\NAME] Download, verify, decrypt and restore into the throwaway container; never touches production. scripts/backup-restore.test.sh End-to-end test: scratch DB, all migrations, seed, backup, encrypt, verify, plus negative cases (wrong passphrase, truncated file); then the S3 round trip against a throwaway MinIO (see below). Run in CI by .github/workflows/backup-restore.yml. Typical cron entry (daily, encrypted, keep 14): 15 3 cd /opt/openfamily && BACKUPKEEP=14 BACKUPPASSPHRASEFILE=/root/.of-backup-pass ./scripts/backup.sh && ./scripts/verify-backup.sh "$(ls -1t backups/openfamily-.enc head -1)" Keep the passphrase file outside backups/ and outside the copy that is shipped off-host (password manager). A backup without its passphrase is unrecoverable by design. Volume snapshots pgdump is the supported path. A filesystem/LVM/ZFS/cloud snapshot of the pgdata volume is an acceptable additional layer, but only crash-consistent: snapshot with the postgres container stopped (or use pgbackupstart), restore into the same image tag/digest, and never mix a snapshot with a different Postgres major version. RPO and RTO Target How it is achieved RPO (data you can lose) equal to the backup interval: 24 h with the daily cron above; 1 h with an hourly cron Location points are re-sent by phones that were offline, so recent loss is partly self-healing; history older than the last backup is not. RTO (time to recover) under 30 min for a typical family instance (a few GB) docker compose up -d postgres, scripts/restore.sh, api start. Restore time scales with dump size; measure on your hardware with time scripts/verify-backup.sh <file>. Measured here: scripts/backup-restore.test.sh (migrations + seed + 2 verified restores + 2 negative cases) passed on a heavily loaded development host in about 9.5 minutes, dominated by container start-up; this is a functional result, not a performance benchmark. Record your own RTO from a real backup at least once per quarter (run verify-backup.sh on a production dump). Restore drill checklist 1. ./scripts/verify-backup.sh <latest backup> prints VERIFIED and plausible row counts (users, locations). 2. Compare counts with production (--source-container against a live container, or SELECT count()). 3. Confirm the passphrase works from the off-host copy of the key. 4. Only then rely on the backup; schedule the drill (CI runs the automated variant weekly). S3 and scheduled backups The optional backup compose service (profile backup) replaces host cron and adds off-site copies. Every night it streams pgdump through age encryption, writes the result to a local directory and/or any S3-compatible bucket (AWS S3, Backblaze B2, Wasabi, Cloudflare R2, MinIO, ...), uploads a SHA-256 manifest next to it, applies retention, and records every run in the database so the admin System page shows the truth. scripts/backup.sh keeps working unchanged; you can use either or both. postgres --pgdump--> age encrypt (public key) --> /work (RAM, ciphertext only) ./backups (optional) '--> s3://bucket/prefix/openfamily-<UTC>.dump.age s3://bucket/prefix/openfamily-<UTC>.manifest.json (written last) Properties: Client-side encryption. The dump is encrypted before it leaves the container; the plaintext never touches disk. The server only holds the public key, so a stolen server or bucket cannot decrypt old backups. Uploading an unencrypted dump to S3 is refused unless you set BACKUPALLOWUNENCRYPTED=true. Integrity. The manifest records size and SHA-256 of the stored object. Restore checks both before decrypting; age's authenticated encryption then detects any modification inside the stream. Multipart, retries. Uploads are multipart (16 MiB parts, automatic growth for huge dumps); each request retries with backoff, and the whole upload is retried 3 times with a size check afterwards. TLS required. A plain http:// endpoint is rejected unless BACKUPS3INSECURE=true (meant for a MinIO on your own private network). Credentials never printed. They are read from the environment or FILE secrets, scrubbed from every error, log line, run record and API response, and are never available to the API container. Quick start 1: in the admin panel (recommended) 1. Start the service once (it needs no S3 settings to start): docker compose --profile backup up -d --build backup. Add backup to COMPOSEPROFILES in .env so it survives docker compose up -d. 2. Open System health > Backups > Settings. 3. Destinations: switch on S3-compatible storage and fill endpoint (empty for AWS), region, bucket, folder, and the access key id and secret. The secret is write-only: after saving, the page only shows Set ...ABCD with Replace and Clear. Switch on Local disk as well if you want copies on this machine. 4. Encryption: press Generate key pair. The pair is created in your browser; the page shows the private key once with Copy and Download, you confirm you stored it, and only the public key is filled in. The server never sees or stores the private key. If you lose it, no backup can be restored. 5. Schedule (daily time or cron, plus time zone) and Retention, then Test connection (writes, reads and deletes a small object using the values in the form, saved or not) and Save settings. The backup service applies saved settings within a few seconds without a restart. 6. Press Back up now, then do a restore drill (below). How settings are combined: environment variables win. A setting present in the backup service's environment (.env) is pinned: the form shows it read-only with a "Set by environment" badge. Everything the environment leaves empty comes from the UI, then from built-in defaults. Every field shows whether its value is from the environment, saved in the UI, or the default. Where the secret lives, honestly. The S3 key id and secret are stored in the backupsettings table, encrypted with AES-256-GCM under a key derived (HKDF-SHA256, label openfamily/backup-settings/v1) from BACKUPSETTINGSKEY, or from JWTSECRET if you do not set it. A database dump or a stolen backup of the database alone therefore does not reveal the key. But the API and the backup service both need that secret to read it, so anyone who has both the database and the server environment can decrypt it, exactly as they could read a BACKUPS3SECRETACCESSKEY from .env. Set a dedicated BACKUPSETTINGSKEY (openssl rand -hex 32) if you want it independent of JWTSECRET; changing JWTSECRET or this value later makes saved credentials unreadable (the UI says so; enter them again). Use a bucket key scoped to the backup folder. Disaster recovery needs the key outside the database. Credentials saved in the UI live in the database you would be restoring. Keep a copy of the S3 key in your password manager (or in .env as BACKUPS3) so restore.sh --from-s3 works on a fresh machine. Network policy. Endpoints must be https unless Allow plain HTTP is on. Link-local and cloud-metadata addresses (169.254.0.0/16, fd00:ec2::254, ...) are always refused, checked again on every connection after DNS resolution. Loopback and private (LAN) addresses are refused unless Allow private network address is on, because a MinIO on your LAN is a legitimate target. Credentials are bound to their destination. A saved key is stored together with a fingerprint of the endpoint, plain-HTTP flag, private-network flag and region it was entered for (inside the encrypted blob). If you change any of those, in Save or in Test connection, you must type the access key and secret again; the saved key is never sent to a different address, so a hijacked admin session cannot point the test at a host it controls to collect it. Credentials from .env likewise pin the endpoint, plain-HTTP and private-network settings to .env (read-only in the panel). Keys saved by earlier builds have no fingerprint and must be entered once more. IPv6 is an allowlist: only global unicast (2000::/3, not the documentation range) is accepted; with Allow private network address also ULA (fc00::/7) and ::1. Link-local, multicast, unspecified and any other range are always refused. IPv6 transition addresses (NAT64 64:ff9b::/96, 6to4, Teredo, IPv4-compatible) are refused unless private addresses are allowed, and the IPv4 address they embed is checked with the IPv4 rules; the local-use NAT64 range 64:ff9b:1::/48 is always refused. IPv4-mapped addresses are converted to IPv4 before any check. Quick start 2: with environment variables 1. Create the key pair on your own computer (not on the server): age-keygen -o openfamily-backup.key # prints "Public key: age1..." no age installed? docker run --rm openfamily-backup:local keygen > openfamily-backup.key Put openfamily-backup.key in your password manager and on a second, offline medium. Never copy it to the server. Only the age1... public key goes into .env. 2. Create a bucket and an access key (least-privilege policy below). 3. Edit .env (see .env.example for every variable): BACKUPAGERECIPIENT=age1xxxxxxxx... BACKUPS3BUCKET=my-openfamily-backups BACKUPS3REGION=eu-central-1 BACKUPS3PREFIX=openfamily BACKUPS3ACCESSKEYID=... BACKUPS3SECRETACCESSKEY=... optional: also keep copies on this machine BACKUPLOCALDIR=/backups chmod 600 .env. To keep the secret out of the process environment, put it in deploy/backup/s3-secret and set BACKUPS3SECRETACCESSKEYFILE=/run/backup-secrets/s3-secret. 4. Start it and test the connection: docker compose --profile backup up -d --build backup docker compose --profile backup run --rm backup test-s3 # writes, reads and deletes a probe object docker compose --profile backup run --rm backup run # first backup now Or use the Backups card on the admin System page (Test S3 connection, Back up now). Add backup to COMPOSEPROFILES in .env so it survives docker compose up -d. 5. Do a restore drill now (below). An untested backup is a hope, not a backup. Configuration reference Every variable is optional if you use the admin panel. A variable you set here overrides, and locks, the matching field in the UI. Leave it empty to manage it in the UI. Variable Default Meaning BACKUPSCHEDULE 15 3 5-field cron (min hour dom month dow; , lists, ranges, /n). BACKUPTZ UTC IANA time zone the schedule is evaluated in (DST-aware). A time skipped by a DST jump is skipped; missed runs while the service was down are not replayed (set BACKUPRUNONSTART=true to take one on every start). BACKUPAGERECIPIENT age public key(s), comma separated (several = any of them can decrypt; use for key rotation or a second custodian). BACKUPAGEPASSPHRASEFILE Alternative: age passphrase mode (min. 12 chars) from a file. Weaker, see "Encryption and keys". BACKUPS3ENDPOINT AWS Host or https://host[:port]. Empty = AWS S3. BACKUPS3REGION Region (auto for R2). BACKUPS3BUCKET / BACKUPS3PREFIX / openfamily Bucket and key prefix. Everything the service creates lives directly under the prefix. BACKUPS3ACCESSKEYID / BACKUPS3SECRETACCESSKEY Credentials, or ...FILE variants. BACKUPS3PATHSTYLE false true for MinIO and some self-hosted stores. BACKUPS3STORAGECLASS e.g. STANDARDIA, GLACIERIR (AWS). Leave empty for B2/Wasabi/R2/MinIO. BACKUPS3INSECURE false Allow plain HTTP. Only for a MinIO on a private network. BACKUPLOCALDIR / BACKUPLOCALPATH In-container dir (use /backups) / host dir (default ./backups). The container runs as BACKUPUID:BACKUPGID (default 1000:1000); it must be able to write the host dir. BACKUPKEEPDAILY / WEEKLY / MONTHLY 7 / 4 / 6 Retention. 0 disables a tier; all three 0 keeps everything. BACKUPRETENTIONDRYRUN false Log what would be deleted, delete nothing. BACKUPS3ALLOWPRIVATE true for env endpoints Allow loopback/LAN endpoints. Link-local/metadata addresses are always refused. BACKUPSETTINGSKEY JWTSECRET Secret the UI-saved S3 credentials are encrypted under (HKDF). Same value must reach the API and the backup service (compose does this). BACKUPSTALEHOURS 36 The System page raises a warning when the newest successful backup is older. BACKUPWORKSIZE 4g Size of the RAM-backed staging area for the encrypted dump. Raise it above your compressed dump size. Provider examples All use the same variables; only the endpoint/addressing differ. AWS S3 BACKUPS3REGION=eu-central-1 BACKUPS3STORAGECLASS=STANDARDIA Backblaze B2 (S3-compatible API; endpoint is shown on the bucket page) BACKUPS3ENDPOINT=s3.us-west-004.backblazeb2.com BACKUPS3REGION=us-west-004 Wasabi BACKUPS3ENDPOINT=s3.eu-central-1.wasabisys.com BACKUPS3REGION=eu-central-1 Cloudflare R2 (use an R2 API token with Object Read & Write, scoped to the bucket) BACKUPS3ENDPOINT=<accountid>.r2.cloudflarestorage.com BACKUPS3REGION=auto MinIO on your LAN (no TLS) BACKUPS3ENDPOINT=http://minio.lan:9000 BACKUPS3INSECURE=true BACKUPS3PATHSTYLE=true Least-privilege bucket policy The service needs to list, write, read (restore/verify and the connection test) and delete (retention) objects under its prefix, and nothing else. AWS IAM policy for the access key: { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:ListBucket", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-openfamily-backups", "Condition": { "StringLike": { "s3:prefix": ["openfamily/", "openfamily"] } } }, { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:PutObject", "s3:GetObject", "s3:DeleteObject"], "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-openfamily-backups/openfamily/" } ] } Add s3:AbortMultipartUpload and s3:ListBucketMultipartUploads if you want failed uploads cleaned up by the client (a bucket lifecycle rule "abort incomplete multipart uploads after 7 days" does the same and is recommended). B2, Wasabi and R2 offer equivalent bucket-scoped keys; scope the key to this one bucket, never to the whole account. Ransomware and deletion protection An attacker who ta

docs.title: Installing Orbitly on Android and getting updates
docs.summary: How family members install Orbitly on Android with Obtainium and receive updates, and how the operator publishes them.
docs.text: Installing Orbitly on Android and getting updates How family members install Orbitly on Android with Obtainium and receive updates, and how the operator publishes them. Family members: install once 1. On your phone install Obtainium (get it from obtainium.imranr.dev or its GitHub releases page, or F-Droid). 2. In Obtainium tap Add App, paste the repo URL the operator gave you (https://github.com/OWNER/REPO) and tap Add. 3. Settings for this app (tap its entry, then the gear): leave Include prereleases OFF. In Obtainium Settings keep Background updates ON and allow Obtainium to run in the background. 4. Tap Install. Android will ask to let Obtainium install apps: allow it. 5. Before installing, check the signature (operator, see below): the operator shows you the SHA-256 fingerprint. After install, compare it in Obtainium's app info or ask the operator to confirm. 6. Open Orbitly. When asked, enter the server URL the operator gave you (e.g. https://family.example.com) and sign in. 7. Permissions: set Location to "Allow all the time", allow notifications and "Physical activity", and when asked choose Don't optimize / allow the battery-optimization exemption so tracking keeps running. On some brands (Samsung, Xiaomi, Huawei) also set the app's battery to "Unrestricted". Updates Obtainium checks GitHub every few hours. When the operator publishes a new version it downloads and installs over the old one; your data and login stay. Android may show an "Update" confirmation: tap it. You can also open Obtainium and pull to refresh. Never uninstall to update. Release file names Releases from the Orbitly rename on are called orbitly-<version>.apk; older ones are orbitly-<version>.apk. The app and package id are the same, so an installed app simply updates. If you set an APK name filter in Obtainium, use ^orbitly-[0-9] (or clear it). A release also carries orbitly-wear-<version>.apk, the Wear OS watch app; that file is not for phones, so do not use a plain orbitly filter. The server's /app.apk and the admin Builds page take the first .apk of the latest release that is not an orbitly-wear- file. Private repo Obtainium needs a GitHub token: create a fine-grained personal access token with read-only Contents access to that repo only, and paste it in Obtainium Settings under GitHub personal access token. On the server set APKGITHUBTOKEN (if used) similarly. Operator: verify the signature apksigner verify --print-certs orbitly-<version>.apk The SHA-256 digest of the certificate must equal the one from your keystore (docs/android-release.md). Also check the file against SHA256SUMS.txt from the release (sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS.txt); the watch app has SHA256SUMS-wear.txt. If the fingerprint ever differs, do not install. Android itself refuses an update signed with a different key.

docs.title: Server setup: adding your own server to a circle
docs.summary: This page is for the person who runs the Orbitly server for their family. It takes about five minutes and has three steps: pick where the server runs, approve on your phone, install the apps and…

headings.text: 1. Tell the server where it runs
3. Use the server (what each person does)
4. Install the apps and invite family

docs.text: Server setup: adding your own server to a circle This page is for the person who runs the Orbitly server for their family. It takes about five minutes and has three steps: pick where the server runs, approve on your phone, install the apps and invite family. The server keeps history, driving reports, trips and the map for everyone by default; privacy-conscious members choose "Keep on my phone". 1. Tell the server where it runs Open the admin panel, Settings > Server setup, and choose: At home: a NAS, mini PC or Raspberry Pi that you own and that sits in your house. The app then offers "Add server" first, because only you can touch the disk. Rented: a VPS or hosted server. The company running the machine could read what the server can read. The app keeps location on the phones unless somebody deliberately adds the server. If you do not choose, the server behaves as rented (the careful side). In .env the same choice is DEPLOYMENTPROFILE=home or cloud (./scripts/setup.sh asks). The setting in the admin panel wins once made. The choice changes advice and defaults only. Nobody is added to anything by it. Rented server: protect the disk Turn on full-disk or volume encryption (LUKS, or your provider's encrypted volume). Orbitly cannot see your disk, so it cannot check this for you. Set OPENFAMILYDATAKEY (./scripts/setup.sh does this for a rented server). It encrypts stored secrets (SMS token, webhook secrets) in the database. Keep a copy outside the server, for example in a password manager. Once it has been used the server will not start without it, so that secrets are never written unprotected by accident. Losing it loses only those secrets, not your locations. Change the key later: generate a new one, keep it safe, then docker compose exec api server data-key generate (prints a new key) and printf '%s\n' "$NEWKEY" docker compose exec -T api server data-key rewrap --stdin, put NEWKEY in .env, restart. Turn on encrypted backups (docs/backup-restore.md). What stays readable in the database while the server runs: locations, speed, heading, trips, driving reports, history, place names. The server must read them to draw the map and notice arrivals. A stolen disk image of a running or unencrypted machine therefore shows them. Disk encryption and a trusted host are the protection for that part, not the data key. 2. Approve on your phone You do not run any command. The server creates its own key the first time it starts and keeps it in the serverdevice Docker volume (/data/server-device, files readable only by the server). The admin panel (Settings > Server setup) shows a short code of four groups. Your phone gets a message "Your server wants to join"; if you do not get it, the same prompt shows at the top of the app when you open it. Check that the code is the same, then tap Yes, it matches - approve. If it differs, stop and check that you are on your own server's address. Only a server administrator can approve. Approving does not switch anyone on: the circle admin taps Let the server do the processing (recommended) and every member then taps Use the server (or Keep on my phone) on their own phone. The card finishes by itself and turns into a green Server is processing. Where the key lives (accepted trade-off): the server's private key is now on the server's own disk volume, next to the database. Someone who can read the whole machine can read what the server can read anyway. On a rented server set OPENFAMILYDATAKEY: it then also encrypts the key file at rest, so a copied volume alone is not enough. The server key only ever receives the server key line, never a circle key. Back up the serverdevice volume together with the database. Losing it only means the server must be approved again. Details: the separate container (advanced) Cloud and security-minded operators can keep the key in a separate container, away from the database. Set E2EESERVERINGESTTOKEN (or OPENFAMILYSERVERDEVICE=sidecar) and follow the commands under Details on the Server setup card, or the sidecar README. The built-in device is then switched off (OPENFAMILYSERVERDEVICE=auto decides; builtin, sidecar and off force it). 3. Use the server (what each person does) In the app, Use the server (recommended) shows four groups of characters. The admin panel shows the same four groups and a QR code. If they are the same, tap OK. Each person decides for themselves and can switch back at any time ("Keep on my phone"; their copies on the server are then deleted if they ask). Use the server: the server keeps your locations so maps, history and driving reports just work. Keep on my phone: your location is shared privately, encrypted from phone to phone. You get no reports unless you turn on phone reports (uses more battery). 4. Install the apps and invite family Android: open https://YOUR-SERVER/app.apk on the phone. In the app create a circle, tap Invite and share the code. Everyone enters it when they join.

docs.title: Operator privacy controls
docs.summary: The switches a server operator controls over what platform admins can see, such as live locations, and how access is recorded.

headings.text: Platform admin access to live location (SEC-007)
Private (end-to-end encrypted) circles and admin access

docs.text: Operator privacy controls The switches a server operator controls over what platform admins can see, such as live locations, and how access is recorded. Platform admin access to live location (SEC-007) A platform admin manages accounts and servers; by default they cannot see where anyone is. ADMINLOCATIONACCESS (default false; set true to let platform admins see member locations) controls this: Surface Default (false) true GET /api/admin/members, /families/{id}/members members listed, all position fields omitted positions included GET /api/admin/members/{id}/history and /history/export 403 allowed GET /api/admin/activity lat/lon omitted included GET /api/admin/ws socket opens (avatar updates only); snapshot redacted; no location, presence or alert frames full live stream Every denied attempt writes an admin.locationdenied audit row; every permitted read writes an admin.locationview row carrying the viewed family so that family's admins see it in GET /audit. Repeated identical reads inside a minute collapse into one row. Tests: handlers/adminlocationpolicytest.go, handlers/auditviewtest.go. Private (end-to-end encrypted) circles and admin access For a Private circle the server holds ciphertext only, so ADMINLOCATIONACCESS neither grants nor needs to deny anything there: the admin endpoints have no plaintext to return, and nothing was changed in that policy. A platform admin can read a Private circle only as a member: their own account must be in the circle, and a browser (admin web "Private circles" page) or bridge key of theirs must have been approved by their own phone and given the circle key by a member's phone. The server cannot grant or fake this (it holds no key and cannot produce the required phone signatures). Approved viewers and bridges are listed per account on the admin "Encryption keys" page (kind, fingerprint, created) and are entries in the key transparency log. A browser viewer decrypts with JavaScript served by this server, so an operator who modifies the web app could read what a logged-in member's viewer shows; see docs/design/E2EE.md ("Threat model of the web viewer"). Use the phone app if that matters. Trusted-server mode If the owner enabled the optional trusted-server mode and every member of a Private circle allowed it on their phone, that circle is readable by the server: positions are ingested into the normal tables and the circle is treated like a normal circle for visibility (e2eeservermember, derived from the phones' signed consents, never a toggle). ADMINLOCATIONACCESS then governs it exactly like any normal circle (default deny; familyadmin or all as you set it); nothing about that policy changed. The admin map shows only the positions the server decrypted, and every admin read is audited as before. A circle without an approved server device stays sealed and invisible to the admin map. Members can withdraw consent and delete the server's copies in the app (Encryption keys > circle > Trusted server); a circle admin can delete all copies (DELETE /circles/{id}/e2ee/server-copies?scope=circle). Retention (LOCATIONRETENTIONDAYS and each person's window) applies to the copies. Location history retention LOCATIONRETENTIONDAYS (default 90, in docker-compose.yml / .env) sets the TimescaleDB retention policy on the locations hypertable at startup and caps what history endpoints will serve. It is the only place the number lives. Each user can additionally choose a shorter personal window and erase their own history (the trail belongs to the person, so it applies to every circle they are in; per-circle windows are intentionally not modelled): GET /me/location-retention -> {"days": 30null, "maxdays": 90} PUT /me/location-retention {"days": 30} (1..max, null = deployment default); applied immediately and enforced hourly (RunUserRetention). Migration 000130. DELETE /me/locations[?before=RFC3339] erases stored points (rows are removed from the hypertable); without before the last known position is cleared too. GET /me/export downloads all of the caller's own data. Retention in TimescaleDB is chunk-granular for the global policy, so rows can outlive the window by up to one chunk; personal windows delete exact rows. Backups are outside this policy. WebSocket origin (SEC-009) /ws/stream and /api/admin/ws authenticate with a Bearer header or the Sec-WebSocket-Protocol token, never a cookie or query string. On top of that the handshake enforces an Origin policy: ALLOWEDORIGIN empty: same origin only (the Origin host must equal the request Host); every foreign browser origin is rejected with 403. ALLOWEDORIGIN=https://app.example.com: that origin is also accepted. No Origin header (native Android/iOS clients): accepted; there is no ambient credential for a cross-site page to ride. Tests: handlers/wsorigintest.go. Geofence accuracy filtering See docs/geofencing.md.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.summary: How Orbitly is put together: the Flutter app, the Go server, Postgres, the admin web and how they talk to each other.
docs.text: Architecture How Orbitly is put together: the Flutter app, the Go server, Postgres, the admin web and how they talk to each other. phone (Flutter app) --HTTPS/WebSocket--> Caddy (optional) --> api (Go, one binary) --> Postgres + TimescaleDB browser (admin web) ------------------------------------------> embedded SPA + /api/admin/ backend/: the Go API (chi router, pgx, golang-migrate). One static binary that also serves the admin web (backend/web/dist, embedded) and the documentation (backend/web/docs, embedded). Migrations in backend/internal/db/migrations/ run at startup. app/: the Flutter app for Android and iOS, with a vendored fork of backgroundlocator2 and a native drivingnative plugin. web/: the admin web source (Vite, React, Leaflet and MapLibre). Its production build is committed to backend/web/dist. docs/: this documentation. scripts/docs-bundle.mjs copies it into backend/web/docs so the server ships its own manual. scripts/: operations (setup.sh, backup.sh, upgrade.sh) and quality gates (license-check.sh, docs-check.sh). Privacy architecture Circles are Normal (server reads positions) or Private (end-to-end encrypted between phones; the server holds ciphertext). Within a Private circle each person can opt in to server help. Read, in this order: Privacy processing ADR, E2EE ADR, Processing on device, Circles. More Baseline audit (historic) Live tracking, live tracking client, live map Reliability, Performance, Maps Design system

docs.text: API overview The HTTP API is documented in the API reference section of the root README: every route, its parameters and errors. This page adds the conventions. Auth: POST /auth/login returns an access token (15 min) and a refresh token. Send Authorization: Bearer <access>. Phones may also use a device ingest key for location uploads. Platform-admin routes live under /api/admin/ and re-check the admin flag in the database on every call. Versions: the app sends X-App-Version and X-App-Platform; the server answers with X-OpenFamily-Compat. GET /compat returns the policy for the caller: status, minimum and latest version, supported window, the server version and the minimum app version per feature. See Compatibility. Docs: GET /api/docs/manifest.json and GET /api/docs/<path> return the embedded documentation to any signed-in user (read-only). Additive changes only: fields are never removed or renamed for a version still inside the support window; a test enforces it. Topic pages: chat, safety, share links, check-ins, bubbles, driving, push, SMS, passkeys, Home Assistant.

docs.title: Naming: what is Orbitly and what is still "openfamily"
docs.summary: The product is called Orbitly (formerly OpenFamily). Everything a person sees uses the new name. A number of internal identifiers keep the old spelling on purpose: changing them would break existing…
docs.text: Naming: what is Orbitly and what is still "openfamily" The product is called Orbitly (formerly OpenFamily). Everything a person sees uses the new name. A number of internal identifiers keep the old spelling on purpose: changing them would break existing installs, signed builds, stored data or the wire protocol, and gains nothing for users. Identifier Value Why it stays Android applicationId / namespace app.openfamily Android updates only apply to the same application id; it also ties push registration and the signing key. iOS bundle id app.openfamily (.RunnerTests) Same: app updates, keychain and associated domains. Keystore alias, release signing key unchanged A different key cannot update installed apps. Deep-link scheme openfamily://join Invite links already shared and stored in messages keep working. Dart package name openfamily (app/pubspec.yaml, package:openfamily/...) Internal; renaming only creates churn in every import. Dart widget OpenFamilyMark, file openfamilybrand.dart unchanged Internal names. Shows the Orbitly mark. Go module path github.com/TheTractorHacker/openfamily/backend Import paths; independent of the GitHub repository name. Database name and role openfamily Existing data directories and backups. Docker compose project name:, services, volumes, images (openfamily-api:local, ...) unchanged Volume names derive from the project name; renaming would orphan data. Environment variables OPENFAMILY, E2EE Existing .env files. HTTP headers X-OpenFamily-Compat, -Min-App-Version, -Latest-App-Version, webhook X-OpenFamily- Wire protocol with released apps and Home Assistant. Crypto and protocol labels openfamily/e2ee/v1/..., openfamily/backup-settings/v1, ... HKDF/AEAD domain-separation strings. Changing one makes existing keys and ciphertexts unreadable. API paths, SQL, migrations unchanged Compatibility. Home Assistant integration domain openfamily (customcomponents/openfamily, event names openfamily) Existing HA installs and automations. Only the display name is Orbitly. Backup file names openfamily-<timestamp>.dump Restore tooling and retention find them by this pattern. web/package.json name openfamily-admin Internal. Local APK cache file openfamily-release.apk Internal file inside APKDIR. Release files Release assets from the rename on are named orbitly-<version>.apk, .aab, .spdx.json, -unsigned.ipa and listed in SHA256SUMS.txt. Earlier releases keep their openfamily-<version>. names. The server picks the first .apk asset of the latest release regardless of its name, so /app.apk and the admin Builds page work with both. Obtainium filters that matched openfamily should be changed to orbitly (or removed). GitHub repository The repository is renamed from TheTractorHacker/openfamily to TheTractorHacker/orbitly; GitHub redirects the old address. The only place that holds the URL in code is app/lib/brand.dart and web/src/lib/brand.ts (the APKGITHUBREPO default and the docs also name it). CI guards accept both names until the rename is done. Keeping the rename clean scripts/rebrand.sh renames user-visible strings, is safe to run again on a merged tree, and scripts/rebrand.sh --verify (run in CI) fails if the old product name reappears in user-visible text. It has an explicit list of files it never touches (NOTICE, LICENSE, credits, this page, changelog history, vendored packages, migrations). A line that must keep the old name, for example a credit to the upstream project, is kept by including the words "Based on OpenFamily", "formerly OpenFamily" or "wheresfrank".
