docs.text: On-device processing: trips, driving reports, weekly summary (Phase 0 of PRIVACYPROCESSING.md) Status: spike, code and tests landed, not wired into any screen (phase 5 does that). Code: app/lib/services/processing/ (pure Dart, no Flutter imports, safe in a background isolate). Tests: app/test/processing/. Shared fixtures produced by the real Go code: testdata/processing/.json. Go fixture generators: backend/internal/trips/processingfixturestest.go, backend/internal/handlers/processingfixturestest.go. 1. What the server computes today (source of truth) Output the app consumes Server code Where the logic lives Trips + stops (GET /trips, trip rows: startedat, endedat, distancem, maxspeedmps, avgspeedmps, mode, speedsource, start/end lat/lon, pointcount) backend/internal/trips/segment.go (Clean, Segment), legs.go (buildLegs, classify) Go, pure Driving events (speeding, hardbrake, rapidaccel; kind, startedat, endedat, magnitude, lat, lon) backend/internal/trips/events.go (DetectEvents, attachEvents) Go, pure; thresholds from env DRIVING (defaults 35.76 m/s, 30 s, 3.5, 3.5 m/s^2) phoneuse events phone sensor upload (handlers/tripssensor.go); never derived from GPS the phone already produces them (driving/phoneusetracker.dart) Effective events SQL view tripeventseffective: a GPS event is hidden if a sensor event of the same kind starts within 4 s SQL Driving report (GET /trips/report: totals, per member counts, previous period, days[], recenttrips[]) handlers/tripsreport.go, tripsreportdays.go, computeReportPeriod SQL aggregation + Go glue Weekly summary (GET /trips/weekly-summary, current/previous per member, safetyscore) and the Sunday push handlers/weeklysummary.go (weekStats, weeklySafetyScore, weeklyDue) SQL aggregation + Go score Not present on the server at all: a hard "driving score" other than the weekly safetyscore; a per-drive score; "places visited"/stay detection beyond the generic Stop list (stops are unnamed, no geocoding, no place matching on the server). The drive/week result bodies sketched in PRIVACYPROCESSING.md 8.4 (score, places, topplaces, km, drivemin) therefore have no server definition to reproduce; this spike pins what exists (see 5). Algorithm summary (all thresholds pinned in processingparams.dart) Clean: drop invalid positions (NaN, out of range, exactly 0,0), accuracy > 100 m, duplicate and out-of-order timestamps (never re-sorted), and "teleports" (implied speed > 90 m/s within a 10 min gap; the third consecutive teleport re-anchors). Segment: a stop is a dwell of at least 3 min inside max(50 m, accuracy) of an anchor fix. Departure needs two consecutive fixes outside the radius with implied speed of at least 1 m/s, then walks back to the last still-looking fix. A trip ends when the device stays inside the radius of a candidate fix for 3 min, or at a gap over 10 min. Movement under 250 m or 2 min is not a trip. In-progress trips are held back (FinalizeOpen=false) or closed (true). Legs: per step speed is the device speed (capped at 90) if reported else haversine/dt. Steps under 5 m (or jitter under 20 m while the device reports below 1 m/s) add no distance. Steps are labelled fast (>= 4.5 m/s), slow (>= 1), still; legs shorter than 2 min or 150 m merge into a neighbour; mode from the 90th percentile of moving speeds (>= 5.5 driving, <= 2.5 walking, else other). Events (driving legs only): speeding = fixes above the limit for >= 30 s (gaps over 15 s split episodes); hard brake / rapid accel = acceleration between fixes 0.5 to 4 s apart, both accuracy <= 30 m, magnitude >= threshold and <= 12 m/s^2 (larger is a GPS jump), the vehicle at >= 5 m/s before braking / after accelerating; adjacent intervals of one kind merge. Weekly: stats per member over [from,to) on startedat: driving trips only (count, sum distance, sum duration, max of maxspeedmps), events counted by their own startedat. safetyscore = clamp(round(100 - 5 n / max(km,10) 100), 0, 100) with n = hardbrake + rapidaccel + speeding + phoneuse; absent when no drives; the phone count enters the score even when hidden from the JSON (as on the server). The report period is the local Monday-start week or calendar month in a fixed UTC offset; the Sunday-18:00-UTC "due" week is weeklyDue. 2. The Dart implementation File Role processingparams.dart TripParams, EventParams, all constants, kProcessingAlgorithmVersion = 1 fix.dart Fix, haversine, stepSpeed, streaming FixCleaner, RFC 3339 helpers tripsegmenter.dart TripSegmenter (streaming), buildLegs, segmentFixes (batch convenience) drivingevents.dart detectEvents, effectiveEvents (the SQL view rule) drivingreport.dart computeWeekStat, weeklySafetyScore, computeReportPeriod, weeklyDue, weeklyMemberJson, reportMemberJson processing.dart barrel Output JSON shapes equal the server's field names (trip row without id/userid, event objects, weekStat, report members[] element, days[], recenttrips[]), so existing models (tripreport.dart, weeklysummaryservice.dart) parse them unchanged. Wrapping them into the sealed trip/drive/week result items is phase 5. Streaming design: TripSegmenter is a resumable state machine that follows the Go control flow step for step (stationary phase, moving phase, one fix of lookahead). add(fix) is O(1) amortised except at trip end (builds legs/events once over that trip's fixes). takeNew() returns finalized trips/stops. Memory is bounded by the retained fixes: from the start of the current stop through the current trip. A stationary period longer than maxStopFixes (2048) is folded into running sums (exact centroid and point count). Deterministic: no clocks, no randomness, no I/O. The caller owns persistence of what it needs to resume (see 6). 3. Fidelity The Go fixtures are produced by running the actual Go Segment, attachEvents, DetectEvents, weeklySafetyScore, computeReportPeriod, weeklyDue. For the SQL aggregations the Go test contains a transcription of the queries (it cannot call SQL without a database); equality with the real SQL is not proven by these tests (see 7). Matches exactly (asserted) Number, order, mode, speedsource, pointcount, timestamps (microsecond integers), open flag of every trip and stop; event kinds, counts and start/end instants. Cleaner statistics (Used, OutOfOrder, Duplicate, LowAccuracy, Teleport, InvalidPosition), inprogress, safeuntil. Safety score (all cases), report periods (week and month, offsets -480..+840 min, errors), weeklyDue, per-day buckets, recent trips and event counts. Chunked streaming with takeNew() between fixes equals the batch result; forcing the long-stop fold (maxStopFixes = 40) does not change any output. Tolerated differences (documented, asserted) Floating point: distances, speeds, magnitudes, coordinates compared with abs <= 1e-6 + 1e-9 expected. Reason: Go and Dart use different libm implementations of sin/cos/asin; observed differences are at the last bits. A threshold comparison that lands exactly on the boundary could in principle flip; none occurred in the fixtures. Times: Go keeps nanoseconds, Dart microseconds. Phone fixes are millisecond precision, so no effect. The server can hold fixes from several devices of one user and interleave them; a phone only has its own device. That is a difference of input, not of algorithm. The server's tripeventseffective also honours dismissedat / passenger marks (tripeventsvisible); the phone has no such state in this spike. Differences by design (not reproducible on the phone) Server Params/EventParams env overrides (DRIVING) are compile-time defaults here; the thresholds actually used must be carried in the result (the server already returns them in thresholds). The server re-segments with a 10 min overlap watermark and a 20000-point cap per pass; the phone streams. With the same fixes the output is identical, with different batching it is also identical (tested), but a phone that missed fixes while the OS killed it will simply have gaps, as the server would for a device that did not report. Only the stationary fold (above 2048 fixes in one stop) can deviate: if the walk-back for a departure needed to go behind the folded region (a sustained >= 1 m/s reported speed inside a 50 m radius for more than 64 fixes). Not observed; documented, not asserted. 4. CPU and memory (Dart VM micro-benchmarks only) There are no battery measurements in this document, and none were possible. The numbers below come from app/test/processing/processingbenchmarktest.dart, run with flutter test (two runs agreed within about 30 percent; figures are from the last run; Dart VM, JIT, x86-64 Linux desktop in a Docker container, shared host with load average above 30, no release/AOT build, no Android/iOS runtime). They bound the algorithmic cost per fix. They say nothing about energy: wake-ups, radio, GPS duty cycle, storage writes and sealing cost dominate battery on a phone and were not measured. A mid-range ARM phone is typically several times slower than a desktop core; treat the figures as an order of magnitude, not a prediction. Scenario Fixes Result One week, 2 drives/day at 2 s sampling, 60 s sampling otherwise 22,260 123 ms total for the whole week, mean 5.6 us/fix, p99 5 us/fix, worst single add 23.5 ms (the call that closes a trip: builds legs and events for ~900 fixes), peak buffer 1,322 fixes Worst case 1 Hz for 24 h (86,400 fixes, 2 drives) 86,400 32 ms total, 0.38 us/fix, peak buffer 3,369 fixes (a 30 min drive at 1 Hz plus context) Weekly aggregation of 1,000 trips + 3,000 events n/a 6.4 ms Resident memory delta during the week run n/a about 9.5 MiB (includes the 22k test fixes and JIT), so not a clean measurement of the segmenter Reading: processing cost per fix is microseconds, i.e. below the cost of receiving a fix from the OS. Buffered fixes are bounded by the longest stop (folded beyond 2,048) or the longest trip (a 10 h drive at 1 Hz would hold 36,000 fixes, roughly 3 MB). No work is proportional to total history, so the segmenter can run on every fix in the existing background isolate or in batches whenever the app wakes. Events and legs are computed once per trip, not per fix. 5. What the phone result items can reproduce, and what they cannot trip: yes (all server fields). from/to names and polyline are not part of the server trip row either (names come from geocoding, off by default for phone-only members; a polyline needs retention of raw fixes, not done by this code). drive: events yes (speeding, hard brake, rapid accel from GPS exactly as the server; phoneuse from the existing sensor stream via effectiveEvents). A per-drive score and phoneuses have no server definition; the only score on the server is the weekly safetyscore implemented here. Do not invent a per-drive score without an owner decision. week: drives, distancem, durations, topspeedmps, events, safetyscore exact. trips/km/drivemin are derived trivially. places/topplaces have no server algorithm (stops are unnamed centroids); the phone could match ProcessedStops to the circle's own places, which is new design, not parity. Not computable on a phone: anything needing other members' raw fixes, reverse geocoding, map matching, the Sunday push for a phone that is off. 6. Integration notes for phase 5 Persist, per device, only the unfinished state: the segmenter has no serialization yet. The simplest safe resume, same as the server's watermark, is to keep the raw fixes from the start of the last finalized stop (SegmentResult.safeUntilUs, minus ~10 min) and replay them into a fresh TripSegmenter; replay is deterministic. A snapshot/restore API is left out on purpose to avoid a second source of bugs. Feed it the same fixes that are sealed and uploaded (the chunk the phone already holds), time-ordered; out-of-order fixes are rejected exactly as on the server. Run in the background isolate; hand takeNew() output to the result-item sealing code. Result items are idempotent per trip startedat (the server upserts on (userid, startedat)): newest wins. Emit a result item only when takeNew() returns something; one upload per trip and one per week, as 8.4 assumed. 7. Unverified, and device measurements the owner must do Not verified here: The SQL aggregations were transcribed into Go for the fixtures; equivalence to the live SQL on Timescale/Postgres was not run (no database was started). A one-off check against a seeded database is recommended before relying on report parity. tripeventsvisible / dismissed events and passenger marks are not modelled. Behaviour on real tracks (the fixtures are synthetic, deterministic scenarios: commute with hard brake / rapid accel / speeding, derived speed, walking, walk-drive-walk, GPS garbage, gaps, in-progress, two drives with a pause, stop-and-go, 12 h stationary, jitter then drive, 30 s sparse sampling). The server's own tests use the same style. Recorded real tracks, once the owner has exported some, should be added as fixtures with the Go generator. ARM/AOT performance and anything about battery, thermal state, background execution limits. Device measurements the owner must do (mid-range Android and an iPhone, release builds, screen off, normal use for at least 24 h each, paired with a control phone running the same app with processing disabled): 1. Battery drain per hour and per day with processing on vs off (Android dumpsys batterystats / Battery Historian; iOS Xcode Energy gauge or MetricKit), for a typical day (2 drives) and a heavy day (4 h driving at 1 Hz). 2. CPU time of the background isolate per fix and per closed trip (AOT release, Timeline/dart:developer markers), and peak RSS during a 10 h drive at 1 Hz. 3. Wake-up count and whether iOS suspends the isolate between fixes (does the segmenter see every fix, or does TripSegmenter get bursts after resume?). The algorithm is burst-safe; only completeness of fixes matters. 4. Fix density the platform really delivers when moving and when still (the events need 0.5 to 4 s spacing; at the app's usual 10 to 60 s spacing hard-brake/accel events are under-counted, same as the server, see docs/driving.md). 5. Write amplification: size and frequency of result uploads and of the persisted replay window. 6. Compare phone-produced trips with the server's for the same real day on a server-assisted test member (both lanes active) and file the differences. 8. How to regenerate / run Go: regenerate shared fixtures (only when the Go algorithm intentionally changes) cd backend && UPDATEPROCESSINGFIXTURES=1 go test ./internal/trips ./internal/handlers -run 'TestProcessing' Go: verify committed fixtures are current (runs in normal CI) cd backend && go test ./internal/trips ./internal/handlers -run 'TestProcessing' Dart cd app && flutter analyze lib/services/processing test/processing && flutter test test/processing A change to any threshold or branch in backend/internal/trips fails the Go fixture test (stale file) until the fixtures are regenerated, which in turn fails the Dart tests until the port is updated: that is the drift guard.

docs.title: Watch apps (companion model)
docs.summary: The phone holds all secrets and sends watches a small readable snapshot; watches send back a fixed set of commands.

headings.text: Decision: the phone is the only holder of secrets
Standalone LTE mode (future work, not built)

docs.text: Watch apps (companion model) The phone holds all secrets and sends watches a small readable snapshot; watches send back a fixed set of commands. Status: Wear OS part implemented in v0.25 (unreleased). The Apple Watch part is written by the Apple Watch workstream and is kept in its own section at the end; the snapshot and command contract below is shared so both watches speak the same language to the phone. Decision: the phone is the only holder of secrets Orbitly's watches are companions. The phone app stays the only place that holds the sign-in token, the Private-circle (end-to-end) keys and the server address. It pushes a small, already-readable snapshot to the watch. The watch sends commands back ("I'm OK", SOS, pause sharing). The phone runs them with its own credentials and keys. Why: Private circles keep working. Positions in a Private circle can only be decrypted on a phone that holds the circle key. A watch that talked to the server directly would need that key too (a new device to approve, a new key wrap, a new thing to lose). With the companion model no key or token ever exists on the watch. No new server surface. The server, API and migrations do not change. The watch is not a "device" in the server's eyes. Battery. The watch does no networking and no polling. It wakes only when the phone changes the snapshot. Trade-off (said plainly in the user docs): the watch is only as live as its phone. If the phone is off, out of Bluetooth/Wi-Fi range, or Orbitly is not running on it, the watch shows the last snapshot with its age and a "phone not connected" note, and commands cannot be delivered. A watch with its own LTE cannot work alone (see "Standalone LTE mode" below). server <--TLS--> PHONE (tokens, E2EE keys, decrypts) <--Bluetooth/Wi-Fi--> WATCH snapshot (JSON, < 100 KB) ---------------------> (no secrets) <------------------------- command (small JSON) Security Pairing is the trust boundary. On Wear OS the Wearable Data Layer only delivers data between a phone and the watch it is paired to, and only between apps with the same applicationId signed with the same key. The watch app uses app.openfamily (like the phone app) and the same release signing key (CI uses the same keystore secrets). A different app, or a differently signed build, cannot read the snapshot or send commands. The watch trusts only its paired phone. The watch app never opens a network connection and does not request INTERNET. Commands are a fixed vocabulary. The phone accepts only the commands listed below, with size limits, a replay window and per-command rate limits. Chat quick replies are sent as an id ("omw"); the phone maps the id to the text, so the watch cannot make the phone send arbitrary text. SOS from the watch needs a deliberate press-and-hold plus a 5 second countdown with cancel. The phone additionally refuses a second SOS within 60 s. Orbitly never contacts emergency services; the watch says so. What leaves the phone. The snapshot contains names, last positions (lat/lon), place names, addresses, battery, and alert text for the circle the phone currently shows. For a Private circle that is plaintext on the phone-watch link and on the watch's storage, but it never goes to the server or any third party by Orbitly. On Wear OS the Data Layer transfer goes over the local Bluetooth/Wi-Fi link between the paired devices; Google Play services on the phone and the watch handle it (Google's servers are not used for the transfer, but the Data Layer is a Google component, which is the accepted trade-off). Users who do not want plaintext of a Private circle on a watch can turn the watch bridge off in Settings, Watch (Private circles can also be excluded: "Show Private circles on the watch", default on, off removes them from the snapshot). Sign-out on the phone, or turning the bridge off, deletes the Data Layer item and is a debt, not a best effort: a persistent clear-pending flag (in Dart preferences and in native preferences) is set first. The clear counts as paid only when the delete succeeded and a watch was connected to receive it. Otherwise the flag stays, no snapshot is published (Dart refuses, and the native publish refuses) until the user signs in again, and the debt is paid the next time a watch connects (WatchListenerService.onPeerConnected / onCapabilityChanged, which also works with the app closed) or at the next app start. Just before sending, the bridge re-checks enabled, signed in and not-pending, so a snapshot being built during a sign-out cannot override the clear. On the watch, a deleted item, an empty (signedIn: false) snapshot, or a connected phone with no snapshot item at all wipes the stored snapshot and redraws the tile and complication empty. Dim/ambient: the watch app shows names and places in ambient mode, same as the Wear OS system does for other apps; no extra privacy layer is added. Snapshot (phone to watch) One JSON document, UTF-8, v: 1. Hard cap 100 KB (the phone drops the least important members until it fits; in practice it is about 3 to 6 KB for a family). { "v": 1, "ts": 1767225600000, "signedIn": true, "scope": {"id": "all", "name": "Everyone", "private": false}, "circles": [{"id": "c1", "name": "Family", "unread": 2, "private": false}], "me": {"sharing": "on", "pausedUntil": null}, "unread": 2, "members": [{ "id": "u1", "name": "Sam", "initials": "S", "color": 4283215696, "lat": 51.5, "lon": -0.12, "fixAt": 1767225500000, "battery": 63, "state": "driving", "speedKmh": 68, "place": "Home", "address": "12 High St", "line": "Driving 42 mph", "private": false, "you": false }], "alerts": [{"id": "a1", "kind": "sos", "from": "Sam", "at": 1767225000000, "note": "", "active": true}], "lastCommand": {"id": "k9", "cmd": "checkin", "ok": true, "at": 1767225590000, "message": ""} } state is one of driving, moving, atplace, still, stopped, none. line is the phone's own one-line status text, so the watch and the phone always say the same thing (units follow the phone's setting). ts is when the snapshot was built; the watch shows "updated N min ago" from it. Members carry their own fixAt (when the position was taken). lastCommand is how the phone answers a command; a watch matches id with the command it sent. This avoids a second channel and is delta-friendly. The Apple Watch uses the same JSON (WatchConnectivity applicationContext). Rate limiting and deltas. The phone builds a content hash of the snapshot without ts; it publishes only when the hash changed, never more than once per 5 seconds (trailing edge, so the newest state always goes out), and a periodic keep-alive at most every 10 minutes so the age stays honest. The Data Layer itself also drops writes that do not change the item. Positions are rounded to 5 decimals (about 1 m). Members are capped at 15. Commands (watch to phone) Wear OS: MessageClient, path /orbitly/cmd, payload a small JSON: {"id": "<random>", "cmd": "<name>", "at": <ms>, "arg": "<optional>"}. cmd arg What the phone does sos none Sends the same SOS as the in-app button (POST /alerts/sos with its own location, sealed position for Private circles). checkin none "I'm OK" check-in to the circle (POST /alerts/check-in). pause minutes (15, 60, 240) Pauses sharing for that time. resume none Resumes sharing. ack alert id Marks an alert seen (POST /alerts/{id}/ack). refresh none Rebuilds and publishes the snapshot now (still rate limited to once per 5 s). reply reply id (ok, omw, late, call, thanks) Sends the fixed text to the circle chat the phone has open (or the first circle). The phone replies through lastCommand in the next snapshot. A command is valid for 2 minutes after at (replay window; the watch and phone clocks only need to agree to within that) and an id is processed once. When the phone app is not running. Commands are handled by the Orbitly app process. If the Flutter engine is not running the native receiver answers the watch straight away with ok: false ("Open Orbitly on your phone") instead of queueing: a stale SOS that fires minutes later would be worse than a clear failure. The watch therefore always tells the user whether the command arrived, and the SOS screen says "If it did not send, call emergency services". Wear OS app Separate Gradle project in wear/ (Kotlin, Jetpack Compose for Wear OS, androidx.wear.compose Material), minSdk 30 (Wear OS 3+: Galaxy Watch 4 and newer, Pixel Watch, Fossil Gen 6, TicWatch Pro 5 and others). Older Tizen Galaxy Watches (Watch 3 and earlier, Active, Gear) are not supported: they are a different operating system. applicationId app.openfamily, versionName/versionCode computed from the release tag exactly as for the phone APK (wear.yml and apk.yml share the formula; locally the version is read from app/pubspec.yaml). The watch versionCode gets +1 added to the phone's code only if Play requires distinct codes for the two form factors, which it does not for separate apps in one listing. com.google.android.wearable.standalone is false: the app needs the phone for all its data. Play then lists it as a companion-dependent watch app. Setting it to true would claim the watch works alone, which is not true in this design. Updates arrive by DataClient changes only (a WearableListenerService is woken by the system; the UI collects from a StateFlow). No polling, no background service, no wake locks. Screens: People, Person (place, age, "Open on phone", distance and direction), SOS (hold to arm, 5 s countdown, cancel, haptics), I'm OK, Sharing pause and resume, Quick replies with unread badge, Alerts. A Tile ("Circle", the people nearest to you) and a Complication (nearest member, unread, sharing state). Distance and direction use the watch's last known location (only if the user grants location permission on the watch) and the member's coordinates; there is no map. Offline: the last snapshot is stored on the watch (DataClient item or a copy in app storage) and shown with its age; the header shows "Phone not connected". Phone side app/lib/services/watch/ (watchsnapshot.dart builds and hashes the snapshot, watchbridge.dart throttles and executes commands through injected actions) and WatchBridgePlugin.kt (MethodChannel app.openfamily/watch, play-services-wearable). Without Google Play services, or with no paired watch, every call is a no-op and Settings, Watch shows "No watch connected". Standalone LTE mode (future work, not built) A watch with a SIM could talk to the server itself. What it would need: 1. A token on the watch: a device-scoped refresh token minted by the phone ("link device", like the existing QR flow) so it can be revoked on its own. 2. For Normal circles this is straightforward (REST + WebSocket, or just polling every few minutes). 3. For Private circles it needs the circle key on the watch: the same approval flow as a new phone, a new key wrap per circle, and an encrypted key store on a device that has no secure lock in many cases. This is the real cost, and it breaks the "no key outside the phone" property. 4. Battery: LTE radios drain a watch quickly; it needs push (FCM) instead of a socket and a much slower location report cadence. 5. Play policy: a standalone watch app needs its own sign-in screen on a tiny keyboard, or a phone-assisted login. Recommendation: ship the companion model first (this document), ask real users whether the "phone out of range" case matters, and only then build standalone mode for Normal circles, leaving Private circles companion-only. Apple Watch Same companion model and the same JSON contract as above; details, the Xcode project layout, CI and the kill switch are in WATCHAPPSAPPLE.md. Status: written without a Mac, never compiled or run. Watch app: SwiftUI, watchOS 9+, app/ios/OrbitlyWatch/, bundle id app.openfamily.watchkitapp, embedded in the iPhone app (Runner.app/Watch/). Transport (WatchConnectivity): the snapshot goes in updateApplicationContext (latest wins, no queue, no polling); a command goes in sendMessage as {"json": "<the command JSON above>"}. The iPhone answers the message only with "I have it"; the real result comes back as lastCommand in the next snapshot, exactly like Wear OS. If the phone is not reachable the watch says so and SOS is never queued. One Dart bridge for both: watchbridge.dart drives WatchBridgePlugin.kt on Android and app/ios/Runner/WatchBridge.swift on iOS through the same MethodChannel app.openfamily/watch (publish, clear, allowPublish, status; callbacks command, peerChanged). Sign-out and switch-off are a debt on iOS too: the native side persists blocked (never send) and clearUndelivered (the wipe has not been handed to WatchConnectivity yet) separately, retries on every session event, and a new sign-in does not drop an undelivered wipe. Every context carries a session id generated by allowPublish; the watch drops stored data of any other session. Wear OS uses the same session idea: native allowPublish creates a NEW session id, every snapshot DataItem carries it next to the unchanged JSON (json and session keys), and the watch wipes the stored snapshot, tile and complication data before accepting an item whose session differs from the one it holds. allowPublish also tries to deliver an undelivered wipe first; the pending flag is dropped only when the delete succeeded with a watch connected (an empty snapshot announcing the new session is added when the app is not running). Not on the watch (v1): complications (needs a widget extension and App Group), live compass heading (the arrow is north-up from the coordinates in the snapshot), standalone LTE (see above).

docs.title: Apple Watch app (companion model)
docs.summary: Status: written without a Mac. No Swift, Xcode project change, plist or workflow in this feature has been compiled, run in a simulator or tried on a watch. The shared Dart side is tested on Linux…

headings.text: Sign-out and switch-off are a debt
What the first CI run must prove

docs.text: Apple Watch app (companion model) Status: written without a Mac. No Swift, Xcode project change, plist or workflow in this feature has been compiled, run in a simulator or tried on a watch. The shared Dart side is tested on Linux (watchbridgetest.dart). Read What the first CI run must prove before trusting any line here. This page is the Apple half of WATCHAPPS.md, which owns the decision, the security model, the snapshot JSON and the command table for both watches. This page only covers what is specific to Apple. Pieces Piece File Role Watch app (SwiftUI, watchOS 9+) app/ios/OrbitlyWatch/.swift UI, last snapshot in UserDefaults iPhone native bridge app/ios/Runner/WatchBridge.swift WCSession delegate, channel app.openfamily/watch Dart bridge (shared with Wear OS) app/lib/services/watch/watchbridge.dart throttle, commands, sign-out debt Snapshot model (shared) app/lib/services/watch/watchsnapshot.dart JSON contract, single source of truth Settings screen (shared) app/lib/screens/watchsettingsscreen.dart one "Watch" row, wording follows the platform Xcode target app/ios/Runner.xcodeproj (ids AB1C0DE0...) target OrbitlyWatch, embedded in the iPhone app Kill switch scripts/ios-watch-target.py removes the target from the project Transport (WatchConnectivity) Direction API Used for phone to watch updateApplicationContext(["snapshot": json, "session": id]) the latest snapshot; newer replaces older, no queue phone to watch updateApplicationContext(["cleared": true, "session": id?]) sign-out or switch off: the watch deletes its copy watch to phone sendMessage(["json": command], replyHandler) every command; needs the phone reachable. The reply only means "taken"; the result is lastCommand in the next snapshot No polling and no timer on either side. The watch waits at most 20 seconds for the phone's answer and then says "No confirmation from the iPhone". Nothing is queued, so a stale SOS can never fire later. Sign-out and switch-off are a debt The shared Dart bridge keeps its pending flag. The native side adds two persisted facts of its own: blocked (no data may be sent: set by clear, lifted by allowPublish) and clearUndelivered (the wipe has not yet been accepted by WatchConnectivity). A new sign-in does not reset clearUndelivered: allowPublish creates a new session id and sends the wipe first (and with the new id). Every context carries the session id; the watch drops what it stored for any other session, a cleared context, or a snapshot with signedIn: false. clear answers true to Dart only once the wipe was handed over. Known gap on the Wear OS side (not changed here): its allowPublish clears the native pending flag without first making sure an undelivered delete reached the watch. A new snapshot replaces the item, so the old data is overwritten once the watch is reachable, but until then the watch can still show the old user's data. The same session-id idea would close it. Watch UI People list (initials avatar, name, "At Home" / "Driving 42 mph" / "2 min ago", battery), person detail (place, address, age, battery, Handoff note), Distance and direction (north-up arrow, see below), SOS, I'm OK, Pause or Resume sharing, Quick replies with an unread badge, Alerts. Dynamic Type is respected (system text styles, line limits of 1 to 2 lines, scrolling views). Offline: the last snapshot is shown with "iPhone not reachable" and its age. Direction view limitation: the arrow is north-up, computed by the phone. It does not turn with your wrist (no heading sensor is read, to keep the battery). A live heading is future work. Complications: not shipped A WidgetKit complication needs a widget extension target, an App Group (or shared Keychain) to read the snapshot, and a second set of pbxproj objects. With nothing able to compile here that doubles the chance of breaking the iPhone build, so v1 ships without complications. Future: a widget extension inside the watch app reading the snapshot from an App Group group.app.openfamily (accessoryCircular: unread or battery of the first person; accessoryRectangular: two people; accessoryInline: "Anna at Home"). Standalone LTE: future work only Evaluated, not built. It would need: a watch-side login (QR or code from the phone), tokens in the watch Keychain, the E2EE circle keys copied to the watch (or Private circles hidden there), a polling or push strategy for a device that sleeps (APNs to the watch), and its own SOS location (the watch GPS). Verdict: worth doing after the companion version has proven itself, and only with Private circles excluded on the watch unless the owner decides otherwise. Xcode project Hand-edited project.pbxproj (no XcodeGen: nothing could install and run it here, and a second tool in the release path is a second thing to break). All Watch objects use ids that start with AB1C0DE0, which is what makes the kill switch exact. Target OrbitlyWatch, product type application, SDKROOT=watchos, SUPPORTEDPLATFORMS="watchos watchsimulator", WATCHOSDEPLOYMENTTARGET=9.0, TARGETEDDEVICEFAMILY=4, bundle id app.openfamily.watchkitapp, SWIFTVERSION=5.0, Info.plist WKApplication=true, WKCompanionAppBundleIdentifier=app.openfamily. Runner gets a target dependency on it and an Embed Watch Content copy phase (destination Products Directory, path $(CONTENTSFOLDERPATH)/Watch), placed before "Thin Binary" to avoid a build cycle. The watch target has its own Watch.xcconfig that only includes Generated.xcconfig, to get FLUTTERBUILDNAME and FLUTTERBUILDNUMBER so the watch version equals the iPhone version (the App Store checks this). It deliberately does not use Flutter's Release.xcconfig, because the signed-release workflow appends the iPhone bundle id and provisioning profile to that file. Signing: CODESIGNSTYLE=Automatic with no team. Unsigned CI builds pass CODESIGNINGALLOWED=NO so no profile is needed. App icon: the 1024 px Orbitly icon as the single watchOS icon (copied from the iPhone asset, which assets/brand/build-rasters.mjs regenerates; copy it again when the brand changes). Accent color is the brand lime. Kill switch If the watch target breaks the iPhone build: python3 scripts/ios-watch-target.py disable git add app/ios && git commit -m "Remove the Apple Watch target from the Xcode project" It strips every AB1C0DE0 object from the pbxproj and deletes the OrbitlyWatch scheme. The result was verified byte for byte against the project without the watch (done in Docker on Linux). The iPhone side (WatchBridge.swift, the Dart bridge) stays and finds no watch. Check the project with python3 scripts/ios-watch-target.py check; re-enable with git revert. Builds and signing Simulator job (test.yml job ios) is unchanged and still blocking. It now builds the watch app as a dependency of Runner, so it is also the first thing to fail if the project edit is wrong. Watch job (test.yml job watchos) builds -scheme OrbitlyWatch for generic/platform=watchOS Simulator, builds the iPhone app and checks that Runner.app/Watch/OrbitlyWatch.app exists. continue-on-error: true for now. Unsigned IPA (ios-unsigned.yml): cp -R of Runner.app already carries Watch/; a new check fails the job if the project has the watch target but the app is missing, and the IPA listing is checked for it. Sideload tools must sign the watch bundle too (see the user page). Signed TestFlight (ios-release.yml): the watch app needs its own App Store profile and an entry in ExportOptions.plist. Until the owner sets repository variable IOSWATCHENABLED=true and adds those, the workflow runs the kill switch first, so the signed path behaves exactly as before. Needed for enabling: App ID app.openfamily.watchkitapp, an App Store profile, a second provisioningProfiles entry. What the first CI run must prove Nothing below has ever happened. 1. python3 scripts/ios-watch-target.py check passes on the runner (it does on Linux). 2. xcodebuild -showsdks lists a watchOS Simulator SDK on macos-15; if not, nothing here can build. 3. The SwiftUI and WatchConnectivity sources compile with the runner's Swift (the most likely failures are small type or API mistakes in OrbitlyWatch/.swift). 4. The asset catalog compiles (single 1024 px watchOS icon, accent color). 5. Xcode accepts the hand-written target: no "cycle in dependencies", no missing file, no "Info.plist" or "product" error. 6. The existing iPhone jobs still pass: flutter build ios --simulator and the RunnerTests job, with the watch app built as a dependency for the matching simulator SDK. Flutter passes -sdk iphonesimulator style arguments; whether Xcode then builds the watch dependency with the watch simulator SDK is unproven. 7. flutter build ios --release --no-codesign (unsigned IPA job) embeds Watch/OrbitlyWatch.app and the IPA zip contains it. 8. Runner/WatchBridge.swift compiles and the iPhone app still launches in the simulator (simctl launch). 9. Not provable in CI at all: pairing, install through the iPhone Watch app, the snapshot arriving, SOS and every command end to end, Handoff, layout on the small and large watch sizes, Dynamic Type. That needs a real iPhone and watch. Risk to the iPhone release The pbxproj edit touches the iPhone target (a dependency and an embed phase). If it is wrong, the whole iOS build fails, including the unsigned IPA. Mitigations: the new job is separate, the kill switch is one command and tested for exactness, the signed workflow disables the watch by default, and the Xcode edit follows the layout Xcode 14+ itself writes for a single-target watch app. Remaining risk: a build setting or phase ordering that only a real Xcode rejects. If the first CI run is red in the ios job after this merges, run the kill switch before anything else.

docs.title: Performance of Private (phone-only) circles
docs.summary: Scope: release 0.23.1 work on the lag reported on an Android phone while a circle runs in Private mode: a laggy bottom sheet, a slow UI, and members showing "location not available".

headings.text: What was found (by reading the code, then confirmed by the benchmarks)
"Location not available" in Private mode: the cause and the wording
On-device reports are an opt-in switch, off by default
Startup and release configuration (checked, no change needed)

docs.text: Performance of Private (phone-only) circles Scope: release 0.23.1 work on the lag reported on an Android phone while a circle runs in Private mode: a laggy bottom sheet, a slow UI, and members showing "location not available". Important: every number below was measured in the Flutter test VM on the build server (desktop CPU, in-memory stores, no platform channels). They were NOT measured on a phone. A phone CPU is several times slower and every store/vault call there is a platform-channel round trip, so the real gains should be larger than the ratios here, but that is a claim about the structure of the work, not a measurement. Reproduce with flutter test test/perf/privatepipelinebenchtest.dart (prints PERFMETRIC lines). What was found (by reading the code, then confirmed by the benchmarks) The bottom sheet itself was already fine: test/perf/sheetdragbuildstest.dart (existing) shows that dragging the People sheet rebuilds no rows. Roster updates are already coalesced to at most one per 220 ms (FamilyService.uiCoalesceWindow). The jank came from what ran on the UI isolate around the sheet in a Private circle: Cause Where Per received item 1 Every received fix rewrote the member's whole stored track (up to 6000 points: decode JSON, merge, sort, encode, write) PrivateHistory.add one rewrite 2 Every item read its circle key from the vault (Android Keystore decrypt behind a platform channel) ServiceChannelKeys -> E2eeService.circleKey one vault read 3 Pure-Dart XChaCha20/HKDF/Ed25519 on the UI isolate (cryptography without cryptographyflutter) ChannelReceiver.process ~5 ms on a desktop CPU 4 Receiver bookkeeping written per item (replay window of 512 seqs, high-water mark, epoch) ChannelReceiver.process 3 to 4 store writes 5 One map frame (and so one roster change, one coalescer entry) per item, also for catch-up items that are already outdated PrivateRuntime.apply one frame 6 replayLatest (runs on every members snapshot) decoded each member's whole 7 day track just to take the last point PrivateRuntime.replayLatest n/a 7 The upload queue was fully decoded three times per change (version check, write, read-back) SealedQueue.mutateOnce per own fix 8 OnDeviceProcessor (trip/drive/week) ran on every own fix, on the UI isolate, for every phone-only member PrivateRuntime.processOnDevice per own fix 9 A snapshot of the roster (REST or members frame) carries no positions in a Private circle, so every member showed "No location yet" until an async replay finished FamilyService.replaceMembers per snapshot On Android the preferences file is also re-read (SharedPreferences.reload(), every key, including the big track blobs) every 2 s and on every queue access; that cost grows with the size of the stored tracks. It is not changed here (see "Not done"). Benchmarks: before and after Scenario: Alice sends 300 fixes (10 s apart); Bob's phone catches up on them in one go (the "open the app after a while" case). Counting stores and a vault in the harness test/support/privatebenchharness.dart. Metric (Bob, 300 items) Before (0.23.0) After vault (Keystore) reads 300 1 key-value store reads 1803 12 key-value store writes 905 9 bytes written to the store 1,868,457 1,846 (plus one track write, below) bytes written, with a full 6000-point track already stored 68,424,556 (68 MB) 228,845 map frames / roster changes 300 2 wall time of the whole catch-up (inline crypto) 1771 ms 1532 ms wall time with a full 6000-point track 5363 ms 1589 ms replayLatest x10 with a 6000-point track 41 ms 1 ms Reading the table honestly: The crypto itself costs about the same (~5 ms per item here). It did not get faster; it was moved. In the app it now runs in a long-lived worker isolate (WorkerOpenRunner, itemopenjob.dart), so the UI isolate only does the cheap checks and the single apply per page. In the test VM the longest stretch the event loop was blocked during the catch-up fell to 21 ms with the worker (45 ms with the inline runner, which yields every 4 items). The "before" run cannot be compared on this metric: its event loop never yielded between items, so the probe timer never fired (maxLoopBlock=0 there means "the probe was starved", not "no blocking"). The big wins are I/O and rebuild counts: 300 -> 2 frames, 68 MB -> 0.2 MB written, 300 -> 1 Keystore reads. Sender side, 300 fixes sealed, queued and uploaded: 2742 ms (about 9 ms per fix, mostly the Ed25519 signature and the AEAD). No "before" figure was taken for this. The queue change (#7) removes two of the three full decodes per change; that is by construction, it is not separately benchmarked. What changed Receiver (privatechannel.dart): ChannelReceiver.processMany verifies a page in three stages: cheap checks and key/sender lookup (once per page), the heavy crypto as one hop to an OpenRunner, then the stateful checks (clock, replay window, epoch rollback, lane verdict) in order. Every check and its error mapping is unchanged; process is processMany of one. State is persisted once per batch. The same (device, seq) twice in one batch is refused as a duplicate. Tests: test/services/e2ee/ (unchanged, green) and privatepipelineregressiontest.dart (worker and inline runner give identical verdicts, including a flipped ciphertext byte and a duplicate). Small behaviour difference: for the legacy v1 item format the sender record is looked up before decrypting (v2 already did); a garbage item from an unknown device is now rejected as unknownSender instead of badCipher. Worker isolate (itemopenjob.dart): only plain bytes cross to the worker (key, ciphertext, sender public key); it starts on first use, stops after 30 s idle, and falls back to the calling isolate if it cannot start or times out. The key never leaves memory except as that message. Keys remembered (ServiceChannelKeys): found keys for 10 minutes, newest-epoch answers for 15 s, dropped when keys were synced (forgetKeys() for sign-out). Missing keys are never cached. History (PrivateHistory, writeBehind): new points wait in memory and are merged into the stored track once per 4 s / 400 points; reads and flushStores() (called when the app is paused) see them. The headless background isolate keeps the old write-at-once behaviour because it can be killed at any time. Catch-up apply (PrivateRuntime.applyBatch): fixes are grouped per member: one history write, one map frame with the newest fix. Older items of the page are in the history but are not replayed to the map. Upload queue (SealedQueue.head): the version/writer check reads the first two fields with a pattern instead of decoding the whole queue. Last known position (lastpositions.dart): the newest received position per member and circle is kept in the E2EE vault (Android Keystore wrapped, same as the circle keys), written 3 s after a change and when the app pauses, loaded once at start (PrivateRuntime.warmUp). It is never dropped for being old. replayLatest now reads it instead of the tracks; FamilyService.replaceMembers puts it on the roster immediately (synchronously) so a snapshot never flashes "No location yet". Heavy on-device processing is opt-in (see below). "Location not available" in Private mode: the cause and the wording Traced path: item -> ChannelReceiver -> PrivateRuntime.apply -> onMemberFrame -> FamilyService.applySealedLocation applyLocation -> Member -> memberStatusLine / MemberTile / PersonPanel. Every place that prints "No location yet" is gated on member.position == null (membertile.dart, memberstatus.dart, memberdetailscreen.dart, personpanel.dart, membermapper.dart, widgetsnapshot.dart). Ways a phone that does receive items still had a null position: 1. Roster snapshots wiped positions (cause 9): the server sends no positions for a Private circle, and the restore was an async replay that decoded whole tracks. Fixed (synchronous restore from memory). 2. Cold start was empty until a fresh item arrived or the track store was decoded. Fixed (vault-backed last position). 3. A frame for a member that is not yet in the roster is dropped (applyLocation returns when the id is unknown). The position is now in the last-position book and is applied when the roster arrives (withLastKnown). 4. When a silent member had a delivery hint (for example "has not received the circle key yet"), the hint replaced the age of the last position. Now the screen says both: "Kin's phone has not received the circle key yet · last seen 3 h ago" (memberStatusLine, memberDetailStatus). Older than 24 h the plain "Updates stopped" line says "last seen 2 d ago" instead of a clock time with no date. The reasons themselves still come from DeliveryHints (v0.22.2). 5. Items that are really refused (no key, unknown sender, old app) still give nothing to show; that is what the delivery hints explain. No code hides a member because the fix is old: the only staleness handling is the grey "stopped" status and the "Position from 3h ago" label (kStaleAfter = 10 minutes), the pin stays. Verified by reading the marker and list code (mapscreen.dart filters only on position != null). On-device reports are an opt-in switch, off by default Owner decision: a phone-only member's phone does only the light essentials by default (send its fix, receive and decrypt the others' latest fix, show the map). Trip, drive and weekly figures are not computed and no result item is sealed or sent until the member turns on "Compute driving reports on this phone" (My data processing screen, OnDeviceReportsTile). Setting key: OnDeviceReportsSetting.kvKey = procset/ondevicereports, value 1 = on. It lives in the private-circle store, i.e. the SharedPreferences key e2eechanprocset/ondevicereports (a file named after it on iOS), so the background location isolate reads the same value. Code: lib/services/processing/ondevicesetting.dart and lib/widgets/ondevicereportstile.dart (separate small files on purpose). When on: fixes are collected and processed in a batch at most every 60 s (onDeviceBatchEvery), yielding to the event loop every 20 fixes, and onDeviceAllowed can veto a batch (hook for "only while charging / battery not low"; not yet wired to a battery source). It still runs on the main isolate, not in a background isolate: the processor writes through the same stores as the rest of the runtime. Running it in an isolate was not done (see below). When off, the "Waiting for X's phone" card now ends with "Driving reports need the server: turn on the server for this circle, or X can enable phone reports." Server-assisted members are unaffected (the server computes for them). Startup and release configuration (checked, no change needed) Release APKs are built with flutter build apk --release (.github/workflows/apk.yml): AOT, no asserts. The app has one assert( and two print/debugPrint calls in lib/; nothing logs per item. PerfMonitor recording is off unless switched on (if (!recording) return;). main() awaits only the stored settings the first frame needs, read together (prefs step in PerfMonitor), and starts push registration and the config refresh after the first frame. The Private runtime does nothing before the first frame (warmUp is started from the map screen's initState, not awaited). Not done / could not verify Not measured on a phone. No Android device or emulator was available; all timings are test-VM timings. SharedPreferences.reload() cost (whole file, every 2 s and on every queue access) is unchanged. Moving the large track blobs out of preferences into files on Android was considered and not done: the headless background isolate has no custom platform channel on Android to find a directory, and a wrong fallback could split data. It is the most likely remaining source of lag on a phone with many members; a measurement on a device is the next step. cryptographyflutter (native crypto) was not added: it needs a native build that could not be verified here. The worker isolate removes the work from the UI isolate without it. Isolate for on-device reports, battery/charging gate: see above. Sealing of the phone's own fixes still happens on the UI isolate (about 9 ms per fix on a desktop CPU, one per few seconds).

docs.title: Google Play release preparation
docs.summary: Where the Google Play listing stands and what is still needed before Orbitly can go public on Google Play.
docs.text: Google Play release preparation Where the Google Play listing stands and what is still needed before Orbitly can go public on Google Play. Current status The English listing is saved in Play Console as Orbitly, with an icon, live-map feature graphic, and five phone screenshots. The short and full descriptions explicitly say a self-hosted server is required and explain how to connect to one. Public production access still requires a closed test with at least 12 continuously opted-in testers for 14 days and Google's approval of production access. Saved declarations include no ads, no advertising ID, not a government app, no financial features, and no health features. The Content ratings and Health apps declarations are actioned. The Target audience declaration includes ages 6–8, 9–12, 13–15, 16–17, and 18+, and commits to the Families policy. The developer confirmed the child-law compliance certification in Play Console. The reviewer sign-in details point to the isolated review family on https://openfamily.frankjohnette.xyz; credentials are stored only in Play Console and must never be copied into this file. Lifestyle category, support email info@foleyit.com, closed-test feedback contact info@foleyit.com, privacy policy URL https://foleyit.com/privacy.html, and account deletion URL https://foleyit.com/delete-account.html are saved. Both public legal pages now load. Data safety is saved in Publishing overview and reports that data is encrypted in transit, matching the HTTPS-only app behavior. The Play listing states that the app rejects HTTP server addresses and directs users to provide an HTTPS URL. No app release has been uploaded or published; the code and public privacy-page changes still need to ship in a release. The Alpha closed-testing track exists but is inactive and has no release. Its country targeting and tester list are not configured. Play Console currently shows 0 opted-in testers. Public production access requires at least 12 real testers continuously opted in for 14 days, followed by Google's approval of production access. Local release-preparation changes add an offline privacy policy before server setup and in Settings, explicit background-location collection and transmission disclosure, HTTPS-only networking, and signed App Bundle output in CI. These changes have not been committed, pushed, or deployed. Validation: 107 Flutter tests pass; Flutter analysis exits successfully with informational lint notices. Release build Package: app.openfamily. The current Flutter SDK targets Android API 36. Use the existing upload keystore; do not generate a replacement or expose its private key or passwords. Never upload a debug-signed build to Play. cd app flutter pub get flutter analyze --no-fatal-infos flutter test flutter build appbundle --release --build-number=NEXTUNUSEDVERSIONCODE The result is app/build/app/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab. Keep the generic server selector: do not compile in the review server URL. The Android CI workflow now also builds a signed App Bundle and retains it as the openfamily-play-bundle-RUNNUMBER Actions artifact for manual upload. Its APK publication behavior remains unchanged. That workflow must run with the release-preparation changes before its bundle can be uploaded. This Mac currently has Flutter and signing configuration but no Android SDK. Local App Bundle generation cannot complete until the SDK is installed and its licenses are accepted. CI already provisions its Android environment. Reviewer server and accounts Use a dedicated HTTPS deployment and fictional sample data, separate from real family locations. The proposed reviewer server is https://openfamily.frankjohnette.xyz. It responds over HTTPS at /healthz and serves the Orbitly admin app; its current family list is empty. Create review-only accounts there before entering access details in Play Console. Do not use real family admin accounts for review. Create two ordinary review accounts in one isolated review family, with one designated family admin. Never give reviewers platform-admin access. Do not require payment, an expiring invite, geographic restrictions, or an unattended second factor to exercise the app. Keep the server reachable throughout review, testing, and later app updates. Enter credentials only in Play Console's private App access section. Do not commit them, put them in this document, or include them in screenshots. Reviewer instructions to complete once access exists: 1. Launch Orbitly and enter the supplied HTTPS server address. 2. Tap Connect, then Log In with the supplied review account. 3. Read the location disclosure and grant the Android permissions needed for the background-location feature being reviewed. 4. Open the family map and People to inspect the fictional review family. 5. Open Places to create a place and configure arrival/departure alerts. 6. Install/configure ntfy as documented for the review server to test notifications while Orbitly is closed. 7. Use Settings → Location sharing to stop this device reporting. 8. Use Settings → Privacy policy to read the policy, and a disposable account for the account-deletion flow. Background location declaration Declare one core feature: family arrival and departure alerts. Suggested explanation: Orbitly uses background location to detect when a consenting family member enters or leaves a saved place, such as home or school, and notify their family. The phone sends location to the user's configured Orbitly server while the app is closed or not in use. Foreground-only access cannot detect these arrivals and departures while the phone is in a pocket and the app is closed. Users can stop reporting using Location sharing in Settings or by revoking the device's location permission. Record the production Android build, showing the prominent in-app disclosure, the affirmative Allow Location action, the Android permission flow, creation of a place, and an actual arrival/departure alert while the reporting app is backgrounded. Use test devices and fictional account names; hide credentials. Upload an accessible video and provide its link in the permissions form. Static listing artwork is not a substitute for this functional demonstration. Also complete any foreground-service declaration prompted by the uploaded bundle, describing the location service and visible persistent notification. Data safety worksheet Complete the form against the exact release and actual configured services. Self-hosting does not mean no data is collected: the app transmits data off the device to its configured server. Do not claim all traffic is encrypted unless the release actually enforces HTTPS for all relevant connections. Data Where used Required/optional considerations Precise location Live map, history, alerts, check-ins Location sharing/permissions can be declined Approximate location Derived from coordinates/map viewport Review Google's precise/approximate guidance Name, email, user IDs Accounts and family membership Account name/email required Phone numbers Optional profiles/emergency contacts/SMS Optional Photos Optional profile avatar Optional Device or other IDs Device registration, push endpoints Used for app functionality Other user content Saved places, check-in/help notes Optional feature input Other data/diagnostics Battery, motion, timestamps Verify Google's category definitions Location can be viewed by same-family members and the server operator. Optional SMS and map providers must be evaluated for data sharing and Google's user-initiated/service-provider exceptions. No advertising or analytics SDK is bundled. Audit records can retain IP addresses after account deletion with user identifiers cleared; operator backups have operator-defined retention. Do not promise instant erasure of every backup. Remaining publisher decisions Build and upload a signed App Bundle; the local Android SDK is unavailable, so use CI after the release-preparation branch is pushed. Choose closed-test countries and add at least 12 real volunteer testers. Start the 14-day continuous opt-in period only after the test release is approved and available. Record a functional background-location video on the production Android build and provide its URL in the Play declaration. Complete any foreground service declaration prompted by the uploaded bundle. Review the exact release and final Play Console changes, then explicitly submit them for review. Do not publish a production release before the required closed-test period and production-access approval. Official references Personal-account testing Background location User data and privacy Account deletion Target API requirements

docs.title: Live tracking: the sending side (phone)
docs.summary: Backend contract: docs/live-tracking.md (in the live-backend change). This page describes how the phone decides how often to read the GPS and post POST /locations, so a driving member's pin moves…
docs.text: Live tracking: the sending side (phone) Backend contract: docs/live-tracking.md (in the live-backend change). This page describes how the phone decides how often to read the GPS and post POST /locations, so a driving member's pin moves about once a second (Life360-style) while a parked phone stays as cheap as before. Code: File Role app/lib/services/trackingcadence.dart Pure policy (TrackingCadence, CadenceConfig, ProfileApplier) app/lib/services/fixquality.dart Bad-fix filter, speedmps / speedaccuracy fields app/lib/services/liveboost.dart liveboost command + "live": true parsing, cross-isolate boost + foreground-presence markers app/lib/services/locationreporter.dart Foreground reporter (map screen alive) app/lib/services/backgroundlocationservice.dart Background locator isolate app/packages/backgroundlocator2 Vendored plugin; new updateLocationRequest call Policy table Inputs: smoothed GPS speed, activity-recognition motion state, live boost, SOS burst, battery, foreground vs background. Precedence: SOS > boost > driving > walking > stationary. Tier Entered when GPS request Post gate (min between POSTs) stationary, foreground default stream, distanceFilter 10 m 5 s idle (background, same spot 10 min) balanced power interval 3 min, distanceFilter 30 m 10 s stationary, background default interval 60 s, filter 0 (native drops to the 15 min STILL profile when activity recognition says still, liveness alarm unchanged) 10 s walking smoothed speed >= 0.8 m/s, or motion state walking/running/cycling/driving 5 s, filter 0 5 s driving smoothed speed >= 3 m/s for 2 consecutive fixes, or one fix >= 8 m/s 1 s, filter 0 850 ms (GPS request is 1 Hz, so never above 1 Hz) boosted liveboost command or "live": true response 1 s, filter 0 850 ms SOS SOS burst (5 min) 2 s, filter 0 2 s (unchanged from before) Exits (hysteresis): driving ends after smoothed speed stays below 1 m/s for 60 s (red lights and traffic keep drive mode; speeds between 1 and 3 m/s never end it); walking ends after 30 s with speed below 0.4 m/s and no moving motion state; boost ends at its TTL (capped at 120 s); each "live": true response extends it by 10 s; no fix for 120 s resets the speed history and returns to the slow profile. Low battery: below 15 % and not charging, and not boosted / SOS: walking becomes 15 s and driving 5 s. Stationary is unchanged. All numbers are constants in CadenceConfig. Applying the profile Foreground: LocationReporter re-opens the geolocator stream (interval via AndroidSettings.intervalDuration, distanceFilter) when the GPS part of the profile changes. A 5 s timer re-evaluates so a boost/SOS expiry or a drive-mode exit is applied even when the distance-filtered stream is silent. Background: the isolate calls the new native BackgroundLocator.updateLocationRequest(intervalMs, distanceFilter, highAccuracy), which re-requests location updates inside the running foreground service (no service restart). Fast requests (<= 10 s) always run as requested; slow requests keep the native STILL low-power profile when activity recognition says the device is still. If the call is unavailable (older native build) the isolate falls back to a full re-registration. Debounce: a GPS-request change is applied at most every 20 s (minApplyGap). Speeding up for boost or SOS bypasses the debounce. A non-stationary profile is re-sent every 5 min in case native state was reset. The service keeps using the existing foreground notification while driving. Not piling up requests One POST in flight per reporter. A fix arriving meanwhile becomes the single pending fix; the pending fix it replaces is written to LocationOutbox and ships through POST /locations/batch (drains are throttled to every 10 s). While the app is open and its own reporter is alive (it marks a shared timestamp every 5 s), the background isolate skips fast-tier posts so the backend does not receive two 1 Hz streams. Fix quality and speed Before sending, fixes are dropped when: timestamp is not newer than the last accepted / sent one; accuracy > 50 m while moving (> 1 m/s); or the jump from the previous accepted fix implies > 70 m/s (after 3 consecutive such fixes the new position becomes the baseline, e.g. tunnel exit). speedmps is the receiver's speed, including 0 when the GPS says 0 and horizontal accuracy is <= 30 m (0 with worse accuracy may mean "no speed" and is omitted). speedaccuracy (m/s) is sent when the platform reports a positive value. Speeds above 120 m/s are dropped. Live boost Direct push command {"type":"liveboost","ttls":60} is handled in DirectPushDispatcher (either isolate; the deadline is also persisted in shared preferences so the other isolate picks it up within ~5 s). Missing / invalid ttls defaults to 60 s; the TTL is capped at 120 s. POST /locations responses with "live": true keep the boost alive. Viewer side: ApiClient.watchMember(userId, {circleId}) and the no-throw ApiClient.watchMemberQuiet call POST /locations/watch (the map should call it about every 15 s while a member is on screen). Coordinates are never logged. Diagnostics The Performance screen's "Copy report" includes a location reporting: line with the active cadence profile and fixes sent (this / last minute). Only the foreground reporter reports there; the background isolate has no UI. Tuning / battery notes Driving at 1 Hz costs noticeably more battery than the previous 60 s cadence, but only while speed >= 3 m/s or someone is watching. The outbox holds 720 points (12 minutes at 1 Hz) if the phone is offline while driving. Idle tier (battery saver) In the background, once the device has stayed within 60 m of the same spot for 10 minutes with no walking, driving or moving activity evidence, the profile relaxes to idle: balanced-power accuracy, a 3 minute interval and a 30 m displacement filter. Reporting never stops (the 10 minute heartbeat and the interval keep running). Any fix more than 60 m from the anchor, walking-or-faster speed, a moving activity state, a live boost or SOS leaves idle at once. Fixes without coordinates never count as stillness. The foreground reporter never uses it. Battery comparison procedure (physical device only) Emulators cannot measure this. The adaptive policy (trackingcadence.dart: still / walking / driving profiles, low-battery intervals at <= 15%, idle back-off after 10 minutes within 60 m) has no measured numbers yet; record them with this procedure and paste results here. 1. Same phone, fully charged, screen off, same mobile network, battery saver off, adb shell dumpsys batterystats --reset before each run. 2. Run A, fixed interval: a build with CadenceConfig forced to the walking profile (5 s GPS) for 8 hours of a normal day (home/commute/work). 3. Run B, adaptive: the shipping build over the same route/schedule. 4. After each: adb bugreport or dumpsys batterystats --charged; note percentage drained, GPS wake time and number of POST /locations. 5. Record freshness: the 95th percentile age of the last fix while moving (must stay under ~10 s) and while still (under ~3 min).

headings.text: Why it used to look jumpy

docs.text: Live tracking: the viewer side (smooth map, follow, speed) Counterpart of docs/live-tracking.md (backend and reporter contract). This page covers what the map does with the fixes it receives. None of it could be run on a device while writing it; the unit and widget tests use a fake clock. Why it used to look jumpy A pin jumped to every fix as it arrived (roughly every 2-10 s), the caption rounded the speed to a whole mph from whatever the last roster said, and tapping a member only animated the camera once. Now the pin is animated every frame from a per-member track, the camera can lock onto it, and the speed is the freshest GPS speed with a short low-pass. Pieces File Role app/lib/services/markermotion.dart Pure Dart per-member smoother (MarkerMotion, TrackFix, MotionSample, MotionConfig). app/lib/services/membermotionhub.dart Owns one MarkerMotion per member; frames (per animation frame) and speeds (per fix) notifiers. app/lib/services/followcamera.dart Locks the map camera to a member's display position, one MapController.move per frame. app/lib/services/watchclient.dart POST /locations/watch every 15 s while looking at someone. app/lib/screens/mapscreen.dart One Ticker, the follow pill, marker layer. No setState per frame. app/lib/widgets/livespeed.dart LiveSpeedBuilder: rebuilds just a speed text per fix and on unit change. How the smoother works Time is always passed in (DateTime now), so it is deterministic in tests. 1. Render about one fix behind. When a fix arrives the pin eases from where it is drawn now to the fix over the fix-to-fix interval (the ts delta, clamped to 0.5-2.5 s, default 1 s). A steady 1 Hz drive becomes constant-velocity motion; chained segments are linear, a pin that was at rest eases out so it does not lurch. 2. Coast when the next fix is late. After the segment ends the pin keeps going along the heading at the GPS speed for up to 3 s (constant for 2 s, then tapering to a stop), then holds. Only when the speed is fresh and above 0.5 m/s. 3. Never backwards. If a late fix lands behind the coasting pin, the pin holds until the track overtakes it. 4. Snap, don't glide, on teleports: a jump over 500 m, a gap over 2 min, or the first fix. 5. Jitter rejection: a stationary fix (speed < 0.5 m/s) within max(accuracy, 8 m) of the pin is ignored for position (speed, heading and time are still taken), so a parked pin does not wander. 6. Out-of-order or duplicate fixes (ts not newer than the newest) are dropped. 7. Heading (headingdeg, or the track bearing when absent) is trusted only while moving, held otherwise, and smoothed on the shortest arc with a 0.25 s time constant (359 -> 1 turns 2 degrees, not 358). 8. Speed: the freshest speedmps, 3-sample low-pass (rising: 75 % newest; falling: weighted mean 0.5/0.3/0.2). Exactly 0 below 0.5 m/s or when the fix is older than 15 s or was already old when first loaded. 0 is a value; null (no speed in the fix) shows as an em dash. Display uses UnitPreferenceService.units (mph or km/h). "Speeding" is round(mph) >= 70, i.e. the number on screen. Constants (MotionConfig) minSegmentS 0.5, maxSegmentS 2.5, defaultSegmentS 1.0, deadReckonMaxS 3.0, teleportMeters 500, teleportGapS 120, stationaryMps 0.5, stationaryMinRadiusM 8, headingTauS 0.25, speedStaleS 15, maxPlausibleMps 90. Frame cost One Ticker in MapScreen. It runs only while a pin or the follow glide needs frames and stops itself when everything has settled, so an idle map and a tab switch cost 0 frames and 0 rebuilds. The ticker is muted by TickerMode when the map tab or route is hidden. Each tick calls MemberMotionHub.tick(), which notifies only the marker layer; it setStates itself, not the screen. The marker layer reuses its cached bubbles and its clustering result. It re-clusters only when the roster, camera, expanded set or followed member change, or when a moving member drifted over 24 px since the last clustering. The followed member is never clustered. The speed caption inside a cached bubble listens to hub.speeds itself, so the bubble is not rebuilt when the number changes. PerfMonitor counters: MarkerFrame and MapMarkerLayer rebuilds (with "Record details" on) and map animation frames. Guards: app/test/perf/livemotiontest.dart (host never rebuilds, bubbles not rebuilt, clustering not per frame, idle = 0) and the existing shelltabswitchtest.dart / markerlayertest.dart. Follow mode Tapping a member marker or a People row centers on them and locks the camera to their display position every frame (MapController.move, no animation stacking). The first 450 ms glide eases onto the member; the zoom is kept unless it is below 14, then 16. Any user pan, pinch or fling (hasGesture) releases the lock. The pill "Following Name" stays with a recenter button (re-follow) and an X (stop). Tapping the name opens the member's details. Follow state lives in MapScreen's state, so it survives rebuilds, the member leaving the viewport, and style/satellite toggles. It stops when the member goes offline (status stopped, no position, left the roster) or when the user uses Locate me or expands a cluster. While following (even if the user has panned away and the pill is showing), the app calls POST /locations/watch immediately and then every 15 s (server TTL is 45 s) so the target's phone reports at about 1 Hz. Calls stop when following ends, the app is backgrounded, or the map is hidden (TickerMode). Failures are silent: the target just keeps its normal cadence. Not done / needs a device Rotating the pin arrow to headingdeg while driving is not implemented (the smoothed heading is available as MotionSample.headingDeg). Real frame times, how it feels at 1 Hz over cellular, and the end-to-end watch boost with the reporter agent were not run on hardware.

docs.title: Live tracking (Life360-style moving pin)
docs.summary: Contract between the backend and the Flutter reporter/map. All changes are additive; old clients keep working.
docs.text: Live tracking (Life360-style moving pin) Contract between the backend and the Flutter reporter/map. All changes are additive; old clients keep working. Data flow 1. Reporter (driving, or while "watched") sends a fix every ~1-2 s: POST /locations (Bearer or X-Device-Key). 2. Server validates, stores the fix (moving fixes are never deduplicated), upserts memberpositions (never moves backwards), returns 201. 3. After commit, the server broadcasts a location WebSocket frame to every connected member who may see the reporter (circle membership + sharing enabled, evaluated per frame). 4. Map clients interpolate between frames using ts, speedmps, headingdeg. 5. Offline backlog: POST /locations/batch (history only, no WS frames). Frame: WS location {"type":"location","userid":"<uuid>","lat":1.0,"lon":2.0, "ts":"2026-01-01T12:00:00Z","lastseenat":"2026-01-01T12:00:01Z", "batterypct":80,"speedmps":13.4,"headingdeg":271.5, "motionstate":"driving","accuracymeters":6.0,"circleid":"<uuid, optional>"} ts: GPS fix time (use for interpolation); lastseenat: server receipt. speedmps, headingdeg (degrees clockwise from north), accuracymeters, batterypct, motionstate: nullable (null/absent when unknown). headingdeg is also in the members snapshot (WS members frame and GET /family/members), nullable. placepresence (members snapshot and GET /family/members only, not location frames; omitted when unknown or location-hidden): {"placeid","placename", "state":"at""left","since":"<RFC3339>"}, derived from the latest geofence enter/exit events (no extra storage). "at" = arrived at since and not yet exited; "left" = last exit at since. Powers "At Home since 3:42 PM" / "Left Work 25 min ago". A fix whose ts is not newer than the stored position is rejected (400) on POST /locations, so the pin never moves backwards. Stationary dedup (unchanged intent) A fix is collapsed (HTTP 200 {"status":"deduplicated","ts":...,"live":bool}, a presence frame instead of location) only when it is within 10 m of the stored position AND speedmps is absent or <= 1.5. Any fix with speedmps > 1.5 or moved = 10 m (radius widens to the fix's own accuracymeters, capped at 25 m, when it is worse than 10 m) is stored and broadcast every time. Rate limits POST /locations: 300 per minute per user (5 Hz sustained headroom; 1 Hz needs 60). Runaway loops still get 429. POST /locations/batch: 60 per minute per user, up to 500 points each. POST /locations/watch: 30 per minute per user (1 call per ~15 s is normal). Watch / live boost Viewer opens the map on a member and calls every ~15 s while looking: POST /locations/watch {"userid":"<target uuid>","circleid":"<optional uuid>"} Response 200: {"status":"watching","ttls":45,"boost":true} Authorization is identical to reading the target's location: the viewer must share a circle with the target and the target must be sharing with the viewer (and, if circleid is given, in that circle). Otherwise 404 (member not found) - no probing. Self-watch returns 200 with {"status":"self"} and does nothing. The watch lapses 45 s after the last call. While at least one watch is live, the target is "boosted". When a boost starts (or restarts after lapsing), the server sends the target's devices one direct push (SSE /push/stream, same channel as locationrequest; also UnifiedPush/APNs silent fallbacks): {"type":"liveboost","ttls":60} At most one command per target per 30 s regardless of watcher count. While watches keep renewing, the command is re-sent about every 45 s (ttl 60 s) so a push-only device stays boosted. It carries NO coordinates and no viewer identity. Foreground reporters without push learn the state from the ingest response: POST /locations 201 and 200 (deduplicated) bodies gain "live": true while boosted (omitted/false otherwise). Reporter should send every ~1-2 s while live is true or liveboost was received (until ttl), else its normal cadence. Privacy rationale Boost only exists while someone with permission is actively looking (watch TTL 45 s, renewed by the viewer's open map). A member who paused sharing cannot be boosted; the server also refuses. Push payloads never contain position. State is in memory only; a restart simply ends boosts. Hot path notes (per accepted fix) Database round trips for POST /locations (moving fix): 1 transaction = BEGIN, device-ownership check + user row lock (one statement), last-position read, locations INSERT, then memberpositions upsert + device heartbeat pipelined in one round trip, COMMIT. The audit-log row is written at most once per user per minute. After the ack, the WebSocket broadcast costs ONE query (own + sharing circles via OwnAndSharingCircles) and no per-viewer queries; geofence evaluation runs asynchronously on a bounded worker pool. Measured BenchmarkIngestMoving (backend/internal/handlers/livetest.go, real TimescaleDB pg16 in Docker on a heavily loaded shared host, 1000-fix runs): about 8 ms per moving-fix POST /locations (full handler, including commit), i.e. one core could sustain >100 fixes/s; 1 Hz x several members is negligible. Before replacing the users ... FOR UPDATE row lock with a per-user advisory lock the same benchmark measured ~280 ms/op on the same host (the row lock dirtied the hot users page and forced a WAL write per fix). Run: TESTDATABASEURL=... go test ./internal/handlers -run x -bench IngestMoving.
